Learning objective: Evaluate which semiconductor material best fits a stated engineering application, and justify the choice using band gap type, mobility, and cost trade-offs.

What to observe: Silicon and GaAs each win two of the five applications shown, and germanium wins the historical one — no material dominates every category.

Full MicroSim documentation →

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter opened the semiconductor category Chapter 6 defined and asked where carriers actually come from. An intrinsic semiconductor's only carriers come from rare, thermally-broken covalent bonds, each producing exactly one electron and one hole; an extrinsic semiconductor is deliberately doped with donor or acceptor atoms that contribute carriers without any thermal bond-breaking, typically outnumbering intrinsic carriers by five to eight orders of magnitude. Real semiconductors split into elemental materials (silicon, germanium — one atomic species) and compound materials (gallium arsenide and others — two alternating species), with periodic-table group number directly predicting whether an element serves as an elemental host, a donor, an acceptor, or a compound constituent. Silicon, germanium, and GaAs each have distinct band gap (including its Varshni-equation temperature dependence), mobility, and thermal-processing properties, and no material dominates every application. A donor atom contributes 4 electrons to normal covalent bonds and a weakly-bound 5th that ionizes into a free electron, while an acceptor atom completes only 3 of 4 bonds, leaving a hole that ionizes just as easily — both processes well modeled by a hydrogen-atom analogy using effective mass and dielectric screening, correctly predicting ionization energies of only tens of meV, comparable to room-temperature thermal energy. Compound semiconductors additionally require precise stoichiometric control during growth, a challenge elemental semiconductors do not face. Chapter 8 now builds on this foundation to develop n-type and p-type doping, ionization fraction, and temperature-regime behavior quantitatively.

docs.title: Key Equations
docs.text: Concept Equation Varshni equation (band gap vs. temperature) \(E_g(T) = E_g(0) - \dfrac{\alpha T^2}{T+\beta}\) Hydrogenic donor/acceptor ionization energy \(E_D \approx 13.6\ \text{eV}\times\dfrac{m^*/m_0}{\varepsilon_r^2}\) Silicon atomic density \(N_{Si}\approx5\times10^{22}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\) Room-temperature thermal energy \(k_BT\approx0.0259\ \text{eV at }T=300\ \text{K}\)

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: See the Chapter 7 Glossary for full definitions of every term introduced in this chapter.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Neamen, Semiconductor Physics and Devices — direct treatment of intrinsic/extrinsic material, donor/acceptor doping, and the hydrogenic ionization model
  • Sze and Ng, Physics of Semiconductor Devices — extensive real-material data for Si, Ge, GaAs, and compound semiconductors
  • Kittel, Introduction to Solid State Physics — rigorous treatment of the hydrogenic donor model and dielectric screening
  • Shockley, Bardeen, and Brattain's original 1947-48 transistor papers — historical context for germanium's early role in semiconductor devices

docs.title: Worked Examples
docs.text:
Worked Example 7 — Classifying a Material as Elemental or Compound

Indium antimonide (InSb) is used in infrared detectors. Is it an elemental or compound semiconductor, and why?

Solution: InSb combines indium (Group III) and antimony (Group V), two different atomic species — this makes it a compound semiconductor, specifically a III-V compound, structurally analogous to GaAs.

Worked Example 8 — Varshni Equation for GaAs

Using GaAs's Varshni constants (\(E_g(0)=1.519\) eV, \(\alpha=5.41\times10^{-4}\) eV/K, \(\beta=204\) K), find its band gap at \(T=0\) K and at \(T=400\) K, and compare.

Solution: At \(T=0\), \(E_g(0)=1.519\) eV directly (the second term vanishes). At \(T=400\) K:

\[ E_g(400) = 1.519 - \frac{(5.41\times10^{-4})(400)^2}{400+204} = 1.519 - \frac{86.56}{604} = 1.519-0.143 = 1.376\ \text{eV} \]

GaAs's band gap shrinks by about 0.14 eV between absolute zero and 400 K — a larger absolute shrinkage than silicon's over a similar range, though GaAs still has the larger gap at any given temperature within this chapter's range.

Worked Example 9 — Donor vs. Acceptor Valence Electron Counting

Gallium (Ga) and antimony (Sb) are both used as dopants in silicon. Classify each as a donor or acceptor, and state how many valence electrons each contributes to covalent bonding versus to ionization.

Solution: Gallium is Group III (3 valence electrons) — an acceptor, contributing all 3 electrons to 3 covalent bonds and leaving one bond incomplete (a hole) available for ionization. Antimony is Group V (5 valence electrons) — a donor, contributing 4 electrons to 4 covalent bonds and one weakly-bound 5th electron available for ionization.

Worked Example 10 — Ionization Energy Ratio Between Two Materials

Using the hydrogenic model, estimate the ratio of germanium's to silicon's donor ionization energy, given \(m^*_{Ge}/m_0\approx0.12\), \(\varepsilon_{r,Ge}\approx16.2\), \(m^*_{Si}/m_0\approx0.26\), \(\varepsilon_{r,Si}\approx11.7\).

Solution:

\[ \frac{E_{D,Ge}}{E_{D,Si}} = \frac{(m^*_{Ge}/m_0)/\varepsilon_{r,Ge}^2}{(m^*_{Si}/m_0)/\varepsilon_{r,Si}^2} = \frac{0.12/16.2^2}{0.26/11.7^2} = \frac{0.12/262.4}{0.26/136.9} = \frac{4.57\times10^{-4}}{1.90\times10^{-3}} \approx 0.24 \]

Germanium's donor ionization energy is predicted to be roughly a quarter of silicon's — consistent with the measured values (tens of meV in silicon vs. roughly 10 meV in germanium), since germanium's larger dielectric constant provides much stronger screening even though its smaller effective mass alone would push the other way.

Worked Example 11 — Interpreting a Doping Ratio at the Extremes

A silicon sample is very heavily doped at \(N_D=10^{19}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\). Find the silicon-to-dopant atom ratio, and comment on whether "heavily doped" silicon is still mostly silicon.

Solution:

\[ \frac{N_{Si}}{N_D} = \frac{5\times10^{22}}{10^{19}} = 5000 \]

Even at this very high doping level, there are still about 5,000 silicon atoms for every dopant atom — confirming that even "heavily doped" silicon remains overwhelmingly silicon at the atomic level, even though this doping level would dramatically change its electrical conductivity.

docs.title: Chapter 7 Glossary
docs.text: Terms introduced in Chapter 7 — Intrinsic and Extrinsic Semiconductors. See the full site Glossary for terms across all chapters.

docs.title: Acceptor Atom
docs.text:
A Group III element substituted into a Group IV semiconductor lattice, completing only 3 of the 4 required covalent bonds and leaving a hole that ionizes into a mobile positive carrier, becoming a fixed negative ion.

Example: Boron, aluminum, gallium, and indium are common acceptor dopants in silicon; boron's measured ionization energy in silicon is about 45 meV.

See also: Donor Atom, Extrinsic Semiconductor.

docs.title: Compound Semiconductor
docs.text:
A semiconductor built from two or more different atomic species alternating on the lattice, most commonly a Group III + Group V pairing (III-V) or a Group II + Group VI pairing (II-VI), whose average valence electron count equals 4.

Example: Gallium arsenide (GaAs) alternates Ga (Group III) and As (Group V) atoms, each bond joining one atom of each species.

See also: Elemental Semiconductor, Gallium Arsenide.

docs.title: Donor Atom
docs.text:
A Group V element substituted into a Group IV semiconductor lattice, completing 4 covalent bonds like the host atom and contributing a 5th, weakly-bound electron that ionizes into a free electron, becoming a fixed positive ion.

Example: Phosphorus, arsenic, and antimony are common donor dopants in silicon; phosphorus's measured ionization energy in silicon is about 45 meV.

See also: Acceptor Atom, Extrinsic Semiconductor.

docs.title: Elemental Semiconductor
docs.text:
A semiconductor built from a single chemical element repeated throughout the crystal.

Example: Silicon and germanium are both elemental semiconductors, each bonded only to atoms of its own species.

See also: Compound Semiconductor, Silicon, Germanium.

docs.title: Extrinsic Semiconductor
docs.text:
A semiconductor deliberately doped with donor or acceptor atoms, whose carrier population is dominated by the dopant rather than by thermal generation alone.

Example: Silicon doped with phosphorus at \(10^{16}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\) has roughly a million times more carriers than pure (intrinsic) silicon at room temperature.

See also: Intrinsic Semiconductor, Donor Atom, Acceptor Atom.

docs.title: Gallium Arsenide
docs.text:
A III-V compound semiconductor (GaAs) with a direct band gap of about 1.42 eV at room temperature and high electron mobility, widely used in LEDs, laser diodes, and high-frequency RF electronics.

Example: GaAs's direct band gap allows efficient photon-only light emission, unlike silicon's indirect gap.

See also: Compound Semiconductor, Direct Bandgap.

docs.title: Germanium
docs.text:
An elemental semiconductor (Ge) with an indirect band gap of about 0.66 eV at room temperature, historically the material of the first practical transistors (1947).

Example: Germanium's higher carrier mobility than silicon's is offset by its much lower melting point (938°C), which limits its thermal processing budget.

See also: Elemental Semiconductor, Silicon.

docs.title: Intrinsic Semiconductor
docs.text:
A chemically pure semiconductor whose only carriers come from thermally-broken covalent bonds, each producing one free electron and one hole together.

Example: Pure silicon's intrinsic carrier concentration at room temperature is only about \(n_i\approx10^{10}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\), tiny compared to its atomic density of \(5\times10^{22}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\).

See also: Extrinsic Semiconductor.

docs.title: Silicon
docs.text:
An elemental semiconductor (Si) with an indirect band gap of about 1.12 eV at room temperature, the dominant material in digital integrated circuits due to its low cost, high melting point, and excellent native oxide (SiO\(_2\)).

Example: Silicon's diamond-cubic crystal structure, introduced in Chapter 3, gives every atom 4 tetrahedrally-arranged covalent bonds.

See also: Elemental Semiconductor, Germanium.

docs.title: Chapter 7 Problems - Intrinsic and Extrinsic Semiconductors
End-of-Chapter Problems: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Semiconductors
docs.text: Work through these problems to reinforce your understanding of intrinsic/extrinsic material, elemental/compound semiconductors, and donor/acceptor doping covered in Chapter 7.

docs.title: Problem 1
docs.text:
Define, in one sentence, an intrinsic semiconductor.

Show Solution

A chemically pure semiconductor whose only carriers come from thermally-broken covalent bonds, each producing one free electron and one hole together.

docs.title: Problem 2
docs.text:
What is the key structural difference between an elemental and a compound semiconductor?

Show Solution

An elemental semiconductor is built from a single atomic species (e.g. silicon); a compound semiconductor alternates two different species (e.g. gallium and arsenic in GaAs).

docs.title: Problem 3
docs.text:
How many valence electrons does a Group V donor atom contribute to covalent bonds, and how many are left over?

Show Solution

4 electrons fill covalent bonds (same as a Group IV host atom); the 5th electron is left over, only weakly bound.

docs.title: Problem 4
docs.text:
How many valence electrons does a Group III acceptor atom contribute to covalent bonds, and what is left incomplete?

Show Solution

3 electrons complete 3 covalent bonds; the 4th bond is left incomplete, forming a hole.

docs.title: Problem 5
docs.text:
Is silicon direct-gap or indirect-gap? What about gallium arsenide?

Show Solution

Silicon is indirect-gap; gallium arsenide is direct-gap.

docs.title: Problem 6
docs.text:
State the Varshni equation.

Show Solution

\(E_g(T) = E_g(0) - \dfrac{\alpha T^2}{T+\beta}\).

docs.title: Problem 7
docs.text:
What sign of fixed charge is left behind by an ionized donor atom? By an ionized acceptor atom?

Show Solution

An ionized donor becomes a fixed positive ion; an ionized acceptor becomes a fixed negative ion.

docs.title: Problem 8
docs.text:
State the hydrogenic donor ionization energy formula.

Show Solution

\(E_D \approx 13.6\ \text{eV}\times\dfrac{m^*/m_0}{\varepsilon_r^2}\).

docs.title: Problem 9
docs.text:
Explain why a broken covalent bond in an intrinsic semiconductor always produces exactly one electron and one hole, never one without the other.

Show Solution

A broken bond and its resulting vacancy are two descriptions of the same single event: the freed electron becomes the free carrier, and the vacancy it leaves behind is the hole. There is no separate mechanism that could create one without the other in a pure crystal.

docs.title: Problem 10
docs.text:
Indium arsenide (InAs) is a compound semiconductor. Using periodic table group numbers, explain why In and As can pair to form a stable semiconductor.

Show Solution

Indium is Group III (3 valence electrons) and arsenic is Group V (5 valence electrons); paired together they average 4 valence electrons per atom, matching silicon's covalent-bonding count and allowing the same zincblende bonding geometry as GaAs.

docs.title: Problem 11
docs.text:
Using silicon's Varshni constants (\(E_g(0)=1.166\) eV, \(\alpha=4.73\times10^{-4}\) eV/K, \(\beta=636\) K), find silicon's band gap at \(T=100\) K.

Show Solution

\(E_g(100) = 1.166 - \dfrac{(4.73\times10^{-4})(100)^2}{100+636} = 1.166 - \dfrac{4.73}{736} = 1.166-0.0064 \approx 1.160\ \text{eV}\). At low temperature the gap is very close to its \(T=0\) extrapolated value.

docs.title: Problem 12
docs.text:
A silicon sample is doped with boron at \(N_A=5\times10^{15}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\). Using \(N_{Si}\approx5\times10^{22}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\), find the ratio of silicon atoms to acceptor atoms.

Show Solution

\(N_{Si}/N_A = (5\times10^{22})/(5\times10^{15}) = 10^7\) — about 10 million silicon atoms per boron atom.

docs.title: Problem 13
docs.text:
Explain why GaAs requires more careful stoichiometric control during crystal growth than silicon does.

Show Solution

Silicon has only one atomic species, so there is no ratio to control. GaAs must be grown with gallium and arsenic in very nearly a 1:1 ratio; deviations introduce antisite defects (a Ga atom on an As site, or vice versa) that disrupt bonding and degrade performance.

docs.title: Problem 14
docs.text:
Using \(m^*/m_0=0.12\) and \(\varepsilon_r=16.2\) (germanium's approximate values), estimate the hydrogenic donor ionization energy for germanium.

Show Solution

\(E_D \approx 13.6\times\dfrac{0.12}{16.2^2} = 13.6\times\dfrac{0.12}{262.4} \approx 13.6\times4.57\times10^{-4} \approx 0.0062\ \text{eV} = 6.2\ \text{meV}\), the right order of magnitude compared to germanium's real measured donor ionization energies (roughly 10-13 meV).

docs.title: Problem 15
docs.text:
Why does silicon dominate digital integrated circuits despite germanium having higher carrier mobility?

Show Solution

Silicon's much higher melting point gives it a wider thermal processing window for high-temperature fabrication steps, and its excellent native oxide (SiO2) is essential for building high-quality MOSFETs — advantages that outweigh germanium's mobility edge for mainstream digital manufacturing.

docs.title: Problem 16
docs.text:
At room temperature, is a typical donor or acceptor atom in silicon mostly ionized or mostly un-ionized? Justify your answer using the ionization energies discussed in this chapter.

Show Solution

Mostly ionized. Measured donor/acceptor ionization energies in silicon (tens of meV) are comparable to or only somewhat larger than room-temperature thermal energy (\(k_BT\approx26\) meV), so most dopant atoms have enough thermal energy to ionize — the basis of the "complete ionization" assumption used starting in Chapter 8.

docs.title: Problem 17
docs.text:
A hypothetical semiconductor has intrinsic carrier concentration \(n_i=2\times10^{9}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\) at room temperature and is doped with a donor concentration \(N_D=3\times10^{16}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\). By what factor does doping increase the free carrier concentration compared to the intrinsic case (assuming complete ionization and that donor electrons dominate)?

Show Solution

\(N_D/n_i = (3\times10^{16})/(2\times10^{9}) = 1.5\times10^{7}\) — doping increases the carrier concentration by about 15 million times, illustrating why extrinsic behavior overwhelms intrinsic behavior at any practical doping level.

docs.title: Problem 18
docs.text:
Explain, using the hydrogenic model, why a material with a very large dielectric constant but only a modestly reduced effective mass would still be expected to have a very small dopant ionization energy.

Show Solution

Because \(E_D\propto(m^*/m_0)/\varepsilon_r^2\), the dielectric constant appears squared in the denominator, so it dominates the result far more strongly than a modest change in effective mass would. A large \(\varepsilon_r\) screens the Coulomb attraction so effectively that ionization energy drops sharply, even if the effective mass reduction alone is modest.

docs.title: Problem 19
docs.text:
A crystal grower produces a GaAs sample that is slightly As-rich rather than perfectly stoichiometric. Predict, qualitatively, what kind of defect this introduces and why this is a concern unique to compound (rather than elemental) semiconductors.

Show Solution

An As-rich sample has more arsenic atoms than needed for perfect 1:1 stoichiometry, so some excess As atoms must occupy sites that should hold Ga — an antisite defect (As on a Ga site). Elemental semiconductors like silicon have only one atomic species, so there is no stoichiometric ratio to violate in the first place; this is a concern unique to compound semiconductors.

docs.title: Problem 20
docs.text:
A silicon sample must be doped so that dopant atoms are no more than 1 in 10 million silicon atoms. Using \(N_{Si}\approx5\times10^{22}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\), find the maximum allowed doping concentration, and identify which of this chapter's earlier worked examples used a doping level in this same range.

Show Solution

Maximum \(N_D = N_{Si}/10^7 = (5\times10^{22})/10^7 = 5\times10^{15}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\). This matches the boron doping level used in the earlier acceptor-ratio worked example, which also produced a ratio of about 10 million silicon atoms per dopant atom.

docs.title: Chapter 7 Quiz - Intrinsic and Extrinsic Semiconductors
Quiz: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Semiconductors
docs.text:
Test your understanding of intrinsic/extrinsic material and donor/acceptor doping covered in Chapter 7 with these 20 questions.

Question 1

What is an intrinsic semiconductor?

  1. A chemically pure semiconductor whose carriers come only from thermal bond-breaking
  2. A semiconductor that has been heavily doped
  3. A semiconductor with no band gap
  4. A metal with semiconductor-like properties
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

An intrinsic semiconductor is chemically pure, so its only carriers come from rare, thermally-broken covalent bonds.

Concept Tested: Intrinsic Semiconductor

Question 2

Why does breaking a covalent bond in an intrinsic semiconductor always create exactly one electron and one hole?

  1. Because they describe the same single event: the freed electron and the vacancy it left behind
  2. Because two separate bonds must break simultaneously
  3. It does not — sometimes only an electron is created
  4. Because the crystal has an equal number of electrons and holes to begin with
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

A broken bond and the vacancy it leaves are two views of the same event, so intrinsic generation always creates one electron and one hole together.

Concept Tested: Intrinsic Semiconductor

Question 3

What defines an extrinsic semiconductor?

  1. It has no band gap
  2. It has been deliberately doped with donor or acceptor atoms
  3. It is always a compound semiconductor
  4. It has exactly equal numbers of electrons and holes always
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

An extrinsic semiconductor has been deliberately doped with donor or acceptor atoms, giving it a carrier population dominated by the dopant rather than thermal generation.

Concept Tested: Extrinsic Semiconductor

Question 4

What distinguishes an elemental semiconductor from a compound semiconductor?

  1. Elemental semiconductors have no valence electrons
  2. Elemental semiconductors use one atomic species; compound semiconductors alternate two or more species
  3. Compound semiconductors are always metals
  4. There is no difference
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Elemental semiconductors (Si, Ge) use a single atomic species; compound semiconductors (GaAs and others) alternate two different species.

Concept Tested: Elemental Semiconductor

Question 5

Which group pairing produces a III-V compound semiconductor like GaAs?

  1. Group II and Group VI
  2. Group III and Group V
  3. Group IV and Group IV
  4. Group I and Group VII
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

A Group III atom and a Group V atom average 4 valence electrons per atom together, matching silicon's covalent-bonding count.

Concept Tested: Compound Semiconductor

Question 6

What is silicon's approximate room-temperature band gap, and is it direct or indirect?

  1. 1.12 eV, indirect
  2. 1.42 eV, direct
  3. 0.66 eV, indirect
  4. 5.5 eV, direct
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

Silicon has an indirect band gap of about 1.12 eV at room temperature.

Concept Tested: Silicon

Question 7

Why was germanium used in the first practical transistors (1947) instead of silicon?

  1. Germanium has a larger band gap than silicon
  2. Germanium could be purified and processed to sufficient quality earlier, and has higher carrier mobility
  3. Silicon did not exist yet in 1947
  4. Germanium is a compound semiconductor
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Germanium could be purified and processed to sufficient quality earlier than silicon, and its higher carrier mobility eased early device operation, making it the material of the first point-contact transistors.

Concept Tested: Germanium

Question 8

Why is gallium arsenide preferred over silicon for LEDs and laser diodes?

  1. GaAs is direct-gap, allowing efficient photon-only emission
  2. GaAs is cheaper than silicon
  3. GaAs has no band gap
  4. Silicon cannot be doped
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

GaAs's direct band gap allows efficient, photon-only band-edge emission, while silicon's indirect gap requires a much less probable phonon-assisted process.

Concept Tested: Gallium Arsenide

Question 9

How many of a donor atom's valence electrons participate in covalent bonds?

  1. 5
  2. 4
  3. 3
  4. 0
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

4 of a donor's 5 valence electrons fill covalent bonds, identical to the host atom; the 5th is left weakly bound.

Concept Tested: Donor Atom

Question 10

What is left behind at a lattice site after a donor atom ionizes?

  1. A hole
  2. A fixed, positively-charged ion
  3. A free electron only, with no atom remaining
  4. A neutral atom
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Once the 5th electron leaves, the donor atom has one more proton than electron, becoming a fixed positive ion.

Concept Tested: Donor Atom

Question 11

How many of an acceptor atom's valence electrons complete covalent bonds?

  1. 4
  2. 5
  3. 3
  4. 0
Show Answer

Correct Answer: C

A Group III acceptor atom has only 3 valence electrons, completing only 3 of the 4 bonds a lattice site needs.

Concept Tested: Acceptor Atom

Question 12

What is the sign of a fully ionized acceptor atom's fixed charge?

  1. Positive
  2. Negative
  3. Neutral
  4. It has no charge
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Once a neighboring electron fills the acceptor's incomplete bond, the acceptor has one more electron than proton, becoming a fixed negative ion.

Concept Tested: Acceptor Atom

Question 13

Roughly how does typical extrinsic (doped) carrier concentration compare to intrinsic carrier concentration in silicon at room temperature?

  1. About the same
  2. Extrinsic is 5-8 orders of magnitude larger
  3. Extrinsic is smaller
  4. Exactly double
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Silicon's intrinsic carrier concentration (~10^10 cm^-3) is dwarfed by typical doping levels (~10^15-10^18 cm^-3), a difference of 5 to 8 orders of magnitude.

Concept Tested: Extrinsic Semiconductor

Question 14

What does the hydrogenic ionization energy formula predict happens as the relative dielectric constant \(\varepsilon_r\) increases?

  1. Ionization energy increases
  2. Ionization energy decreases, since \(\varepsilon_r\) appears squared in the denominator
  3. Ionization energy is unaffected by \(\varepsilon_r\)
  4. The formula becomes undefined
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Since \(E_D\propto(m^*/m_0)/\varepsilon_r^2\), a larger dielectric constant strongly screens the Coulomb attraction and shrinks the predicted ionization energy.

Concept Tested: Donor Atom

Question 15

Approximately how large are typical measured donor/acceptor ionization energies in silicon?

  1. Tens of meV
  2. Several eV
  3. Exactly 13.6 eV
  4. Zero
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

Measured values are typically tens of meV (e.g. ~45 meV for phosphorus or boron in silicon), comparable to room-temperature thermal energy.

Concept Tested: Acceptor Atom

Question 16

Even at a heavy doping concentration of 10^19 cm^-3 in silicon, roughly what fraction of atoms are dopant atoms?

  1. About half
  2. Roughly 1 in 5,000
  3. Almost all of them
  4. Exactly zero
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

With silicon's atomic density of 5×10^22 cm^-3, a doping level of 10^19 cm^-3 gives a ratio of about 5,000 silicon atoms per dopant atom.

Concept Tested: Extrinsic Semiconductor

Question 17

What is an antisite defect, as introduced in this chapter?

  1. A missing atom
  2. The wrong species occupying a lattice site in a compound semiconductor
  3. A broken covalent bond in silicon
  4. A dopant atom that has not yet ionized
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

An antisite defect occurs when a compound semiconductor's species is misplaced — e.g. a Ga atom occupying an As site in GaAs — typically from off-stoichiometry growth.

Concept Tested: Compound Semiconductor

Question 18

Which material has the highest melting point among silicon, germanium, and GaAs?

  1. Germanium
  2. GaAs
  3. Silicon
  4. They are all equal
Show Answer

Correct Answer: C

Silicon has the highest melting point (1414°C) of the three, giving it the widest thermal processing window.

Concept Tested: Silicon

Question 19

According to the Varshni equation, what happens to a semiconductor's band gap as temperature increases?

  1. It increases
  2. It decreases
  3. It stays exactly constant
  4. It becomes negative at any positive temperature
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

The Varshni equation predicts a shrinking band gap with rising temperature, due to lattice expansion and increased atomic vibration.

Concept Tested: Silicon

Question 20

Which chapter builds directly on this chapter's donor/acceptor foundation to develop n-type and p-type doping quantitatively?

  1. Chapter 8
  2. Chapter 3
  3. Chapter 1
  4. No later chapter uses this material
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

Chapter 8, "Doping, Ionization, and Temperature Regimes," builds directly on this chapter's donor/acceptor foundation.

Concept Tested: Donor Atom

docs.title: Chapter 8: Doping, Ionization, and Temperature Regimes
docs.text:
Chapter Overview (click to expand)

Chapter 7 introduced donor and acceptor atoms as the source of carriers in an extrinsic semiconductor, and the hydrogenic model that predicts their ionization energies. This chapter turns that qualitative picture into a working, temperature-dependent model. Doping a crystal with donors produces n-type material; doping with acceptors produces p-type material — but dopant atoms are not always fully ionized, and how many actually are depends on temperature through the dopant's ionization energy. Tracking a doped sample's carrier concentration across its full temperature range reveals three distinct behaviors — the freeze-out, extrinsic, and intrinsic regions — and two further complications, compensated doping (donors and acceptors both present) and degenerate doping (so heavy that simple approximations break down), round out the practical picture this chapter builds.

Key Takeaways:

  1. N-type material (donor-doped) has electrons as its majority carrier; p-type material (acceptor-doped) has holes as its majority carrier.
  2. Dopant ionization is not automatically complete: the fraction of ionized donors or acceptors depends on temperature relative to the dopant's ionization energy, the same hydrogenic quantity Chapter 7 introduced.
  3. Doping concentration (\(N_D\) or \(N_A\)) sets the majority carrier concentration only once dopants are (nearly) fully ionized — the extrinsic region.
  4. A compensated semiconductor contains both donor and acceptor atoms simultaneously; majority carrier type and concentration follow the net doping, \(N_D-N_A\) or \(N_A-N_D\), not either concentration alone.
  5. Three temperature regions describe a doped semiconductor's carrier concentration: the low-temperature freeze-out regime (dopants not yet ionized), the moderate-temperature extrinsic temperature region (dopants fully ionized, carrier concentration ≈ doping level), and the high-temperature intrinsic temperature region (thermal generation overwhelms doping entirely).
  6. A degenerate semiconductor is doped so heavily that the Fermi level is pushed to or past the conduction (or valence) band edge, invalidating the simplified carrier-statistics approximations used in Chapters 9-10.
  7. This chapter's temperature-regime and ionization framework is the direct qualitative foundation for Chapters 9-10's quantitative carrier-concentration equations.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Distinguish n-type from p-type doping by majority carrier sign
  • Explain why dopant ionization is temperature-dependent, and estimate a dopant's characteristic ionization fraction at a given temperature
  • Relate doping concentration to majority carrier concentration in the extrinsic (fully-ionized) region
  • Compute net doping and majority carrier type for a compensated semiconductor
  • Identify the freeze-out, extrinsic, and intrinsic temperature regions from a carrier-concentration-vs-temperature curve, and explain the physical mechanism behind each
  • Explain what makes a semiconductor "degenerate," and why heavy doping invalidates simple non-degenerate approximations
  • Solve worked and practice problems combining these ideas, in preparation for Chapter 9's quantitative carrier-concentration statistics

How to read this chapter

This chapter is the bridge between Chapter 7's qualitative donor/acceptor picture and Chapters 9-10's exact carrier-concentration mathematics. Several formulas here (the ionization-fraction sigmoid, the degenerate-regime criterion) are deliberately simplified or previewed rather than rigorously derived — they are flagged clearly wherever this occurs. Focus on the qualitative shape of each result (why the curve looks the way it does) rather than memorizing the simplified formulas themselves; the exact versions come later.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Chapter 7 established that doping a semiconductor with donor or acceptor atoms creates carriers without relying on rare thermal bond-breaking, and that both donor and acceptor ionization are well described by a hydrogen-atom analogy predicting ionization energies of only tens of millielectron-volts. This chapter asks the natural next questions: what do we call the resulting doped material, how completely are those dopants actually ionized at a given temperature, and what happens to carrier concentration across a doped sample's entire operating temperature range?

The naming is straightforward: a crystal doped with donors is called n-type material, since its majority carriers are negatively-charged electrons; a crystal doped with acceptors is called p-type material, since its majority carriers are positively-charged holes. Real fabrication, however, often introduces both donor and acceptor atoms into the same region — deliberately, through sequential doping steps, or unintentionally, through contamination — producing a compensated semiconductor whose behavior depends on the net doping rather than either concentration alone.

The ionization question is more subtle. Chapter 7 showed that a donor's fifth electron (or an acceptor's hole) is only weakly bound, with an ionization energy of a few tens of meV — but "weakly bound" does not mean "always ionized." At sufficiently low temperature, thermal energy is not enough to ionize most dopant atoms at all, a condition called freeze-out. As temperature rises, more and more dopants ionize, until — at ordinary operating temperatures — essentially all of them are, and carrier concentration levels off at approximately the doping concentration itself, the extrinsic temperature region. Push temperature high enough, and thermally-generated intrinsic carriers (Chapter 7's electron-hole pairs) eventually outnumber the fixed doping concentration entirely, returning the material to intrinsic-like behavior — the intrinsic temperature region. Tracing carrier concentration across all three regions produces one of the most important diagnostic plots in semiconductor physics.

Finally, this chapter previews a limit on how far doping can be pushed before the simple pictures built so far break down. At very high doping concentrations, comparable to or exceeding the density of available states near a band edge, the Fermi level itself is pushed to, or past, the band edge — a degenerate semiconductor, where the material begins to behave somewhat like a metal and the non-degenerate approximations underlying Chapters 9-10's carrier-concentration equations no longer apply.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 10 concepts from the learning graph:

  1. N-Type Doping
  2. P-Type Doping
  3. Dopant Ionization
  4. Ionization Energy
  5. Doping Concentration
  6. Compensated Semiconductor
  7. Degenerate Semiconductor
  8. Freeze-Out Regime
  9. Extrinsic Temperature Region
  10. Intrinsic Temperature Region

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: This chapter builds directly on Chapter 7: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Semiconductors, particularly donor and acceptor atoms, the hydrogenic ionization-energy model, and the intrinsic-vs-extrinsic carrier-concentration comparison.

docs.title: Naming Material by Majority Carrier
docs.text:
Chapter 7 showed that a donor atom contributes a free electron and an acceptor atom contributes a hole, each without breaking any covalent bond. The resulting doped material is named directly after which carrier dominates: n-type material is doped predominantly with donors, so free electrons are its majority carrier (with holes present only in small numbers, as minority carriers); p-type material is doped predominantly with acceptors, so holes are its majority carrier (with electrons as minority carriers).

Doping type Dominant dopant Majority carrier Minority carrier n-type Donor (Group V) Free electron Hole p-type Acceptor (Group III) Hole Free electron

In the extrinsic temperature region (defined precisely later in this chapter), majority carrier concentration is set almost entirely by doping concentration: an n-type sample doped at \(N_D\) has majority electron concentration \(n_0\approx N_D\), and a p-type sample doped at \(N_A\) has majority hole concentration \(p_0\approx N_A\). Minority carrier concentration, by contrast, remains tiny — set by the much smaller intrinsic carrier concentration, a relationship Chapter 9's mass-action law makes precise.

flowchart LR
    A["Doped Silicon Crystal"] --> B{"Which dopant<br/>dominates?"}
    B -- "Donor (Group V)" --> C["n-type<br/>majority: electrons"]
    B -- "Acceptor (Group III)" --> D["p-type<br/>majority: holes"]
    C --> E["Minority carrier:<br/>holes (small)"]
    D --> F["Minority carrier:<br/>electrons (small)"]

Concept Check

A silicon sample is doped only with boron. Is it n-type or p-type, and what is its majority carrier?

Concept Check — click to reveal answer

Boron is a Group III acceptor, so the sample is p-type, and its majority carrier is holes.

docs.title: Diagram: Majority and Minority Carrier Explorer
docs.text:
How to use this MicroSim

Instructions: Drag the single slider continuously from "Strongly p-type" through "Intrinsic" to "Strongly n-type" (or pick a preset), and watch the electron (n) and hole (p) bars and the schematic population panel respond together.

Learning objective: Predict how hole concentration changes when electron concentration changes at equilibrium, and identify majority vs. minority carriers directly from a doping level.

What to observe: The product \(n\times p\) shown in the title never changes, no matter where the slider sits — increasing one carrier's concentration always decreases the other by exactly the same factor, a direct preview of Chapter 9's mass-action law \(np=n_i^2\).

Full MicroSim documentation →

docs.title: Not All Dopants Are Always Ionized
docs.text:
Dopant ionization is the process by which a donor releases its weakly-bound electron (or an acceptor captures a neighboring electron, releasing a hole), covered structurally in Chapter 7. What Chapter 7 left open is how much ionization actually occurs at a given temperature — and the answer depends directly on the dopant's ionization energy, \(E_D\) (or \(E_A\) for an acceptor), the same hydrogenic quantity introduced in Chapter 7's hydrogen-atom analogy.

At very low temperature, thermal energy \(k_BT\) is far smaller than \(E_D\), and only a small fraction of dopant atoms have enough energy to ionize — most remain frozen out, still holding their weakly-bound electron or hole. As temperature rises, \(k_BT\) grows relative to \(E_D\), and the ionized fraction rises correspondingly, eventually approaching 1 (essentially complete ionization) once \(k_BT\) comfortably exceeds \(E_D\).

docs.title: Diagram: Dopant Ionization Fraction vs. Temperature Explorer
docs.text:
How to use this MicroSim

Instructions: Drag the temperature marker across the plotted curve, choose a donor or acceptor dopant preset (or adjust the ionization-energy slider directly), and watch the companion energy-level diagram on the right animate carriers escaping into the band.

Learning objective: Interpret an ionization-fraction curve, explain how ionization energy controls the temperature at which dopants become mostly ionized, and connect the curve directly to the underlying energy-level picture.

What to observe: A larger ionization energy shifts the entire curve toward higher temperature — a more tightly-bound dopant requires more thermal energy before it substantially ionizes. The number of freed carriers drawn in the energy-level diagram always matches the curve's current value.

Full MicroSim documentation →

Recall from Chapter 7's hydrogenic ionization energy calculator and dopant ionization energy chart that measured donor/acceptor ionization energies in silicon are typically tens of meV — comparable to room-temperature thermal energy, \(k_BT\approx26\) meV at \(T=300\) K. This is precisely why "complete ionization" is such a good approximation at and above room temperature for ordinary doping levels, and precisely why it fails at cryogenic temperatures.

Worked Example 1 — Estimating Ionization at Low Temperature

A phosphorus-doped silicon sample is cooled to \(T=77\) K (liquid nitrogen temperature), where \(k_BT\approx6.6\) meV. Phosphorus's ionization energy in silicon is about 45 meV. Is this sample likely to show significant freeze-out?

Solution: Since \(k_BT\approx6.6\) meV is much smaller than \(E_D=45\) meV (\(E_D/k_BT\approx6.8\)), thermal energy is far from sufficient to ionize most donor atoms — this sample is deep in the freeze-out regime, with a significantly reduced free electron concentration compared to \(N_D\).

docs.title: Doping Concentration and the Extrinsic Approximation
Setting Majority Carrier Concentration
docs.text:
Doping concentration — \(N_D\) for donors, \(N_A\) for acceptors, typically expressed in atoms per cm\(^3\) — is the single most important design parameter in a doped semiconductor, because it sets the majority carrier concentration once dopants are fully ionized. Chapter 7's doping concentration scale visualizer already showed just how dilute doping is relative to the host crystal's own atomic density; this chapter adds the temperature dimension, since \(n_0\approx N_D\) is only accurate in the extrinsic temperature region defined below, not at every temperature.

Full MicroSim documentation → Doping Concentration Scale Visualizer (introduced in Chapter 7 — revisit it here to recall how doping concentration compares to host atomic density before this chapter adds temperature dependence)

Worked Example 2 — Majority Carrier Concentration in the Extrinsic Region

A silicon sample is doped with arsenic at \(N_D=2\times10^{16}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\) and operated at room temperature, well within the extrinsic region. Estimate its majority electron concentration.

Solution: In the extrinsic region, dopants are essentially fully ionized, so \(n_0\approx N_D=2\times10^{16}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\).

docs.title: When Both Donors and Acceptors Are Present
docs.text:
A compensated semiconductor contains both donor and acceptor atoms in the same region of crystal — whether introduced deliberately (a common fabrication technique, where a lightly p-type region is locally converted to n-type by adding enough donors to outnumber the existing acceptors, or vice versa) or unintentionally, through contamination during growth or processing. Because a donor's free electron and an acceptor's hole can recombine with each other, only the difference between the two concentrations — the net doping — determines the majority carrier type and its concentration.

\[ N_{\text{net}} = N_D - N_A \]

If \(N_{\text{net}}>0\) (more donors than acceptors), the material is net n-type with majority electron concentration approximately \(N_D-N_A\); if \(N_{\text{net}}<0\), the material is net p-type with majority hole concentration approximately \(N_A-N_D\). If the two concentrations are exactly equal, the donor and acceptor contributions cancel completely, and the material behaves as if intrinsic despite containing large numbers of both dopant species.

docs.title: Diagram: Compensated Semiconductor Explorer
docs.text:
How to use this MicroSim

Instructions: Adjust the \(N_D\) and \(N_A\) sliders independently (or pick a preset) and watch the signed net-doping gauge, the majority-carrier badge, and the approximate Fermi-level indicator all update together.

Learning objective: Compute net doping from independent donor and acceptor concentrations, determine the resulting majority carrier type, and connect that result to a qualitative shift in Fermi level position.

What to observe: As \(N_D\) and \(N_A\) approach each other, the net doping shrinks toward zero, regardless of how large either individual concentration is — the badge switches from "Net n-type" through "Compensated" to "Net p-type" as the gauge marker crosses center.

Full MicroSim documentation →

Worked Example 3 — Net Doping in a Compensated Sample

A silicon region is doped with both phosphorus (\(N_D=8\times10^{15}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\)) and boron (\(N_A=5\times10^{15}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\)). Find the net doping and the resulting material type.

Solution: \(N_{\text{net}}=N_D-N_A=8\times10^{15}-5\times10^{15}=3\times10^{15}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\). Since this is positive, the material is net n-type, with majority electron concentration approximately \(3\times10^{15}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\) — far less than either individual dopant concentration alone.

docs.title: Temperature Regions: Freeze-Out, Extrinsic, and Intrinsic
Three Regimes, One Curve
docs.text:
Combining this chapter's ionization-fraction picture with Chapter 7's intrinsic carrier generation produces one of semiconductor physics's most important diagnostic plots: carrier concentration plotted against temperature for a fixed doping level. Three distinct regions appear, each dominated by a different physical mechanism.

Region Temperature range Dominant mechanism Carrier concentration behavior Freeze-Out Regime Low T Dopants not yet thermally ionized Rises steeply with T as ionization fraction increases Extrinsic Temperature Region Moderate T Dopants (nearly) fully ionized Flat plateau, \(n_0\approx N_D\) Intrinsic Temperature Region High T Thermal (intrinsic) generation dominates Rises steeply again as \(n_i(T)\) exceeds \(N_D\)

At low temperature (the freeze-out regime), most dopant atoms are un-ionized, so carrier concentration is well below the doping level and rises quickly as temperature increases and ionization proceeds. Once temperature is high enough that essentially all dopants are ionized but not yet high enough for significant intrinsic generation, carrier concentration levels off at approximately \(N_D\) — the extrinsic temperature region, the regime nearly every practical device is designed to operate in, since carrier concentration here is stable and set by design (doping level) rather than by temperature. Push temperature high enough, and Chapter 7's thermally-generated intrinsic carriers — which grow exponentially with temperature — eventually exceed the fixed doping concentration entirely, returning the material to intrinsic-like behavior in the intrinsic temperature region.

docs.title: Diagram: Carrier Concentration vs. Temperature (Three Regions) Explorer
docs.text:
How to use this MicroSim

Instructions: Drag the temperature slider (or pick a 50 K / 77 K / 300 K / 500 K / 800 K preset) and watch the region badge, the "why" explanation, and every numeric readout update together; then adjust the \(N_D\) and \(E_D\) sliders and notice the shaded region boundaries move with them.

Learning objective: Identify all three temperature regions from a carrier-concentration curve, explain — in numbers — why the sample is in a given region, and explain how doping concentration and ionization energy shift each region's boundaries.

What to observe: Increasing \(N_D\) raises the extrinsic plateau and pushes the intrinsic region's onset to a higher temperature (a heavier-doped sample stays extrinsic longer); increasing \(E_D\) stretches the freeze-out region to higher temperature. The region boundaries are computed live from your slider values, not fixed in place.

Full MicroSim documentation →

Concept Check

Why do device engineers generally design circuits to operate within the extrinsic temperature region rather than the freeze-out or intrinsic regions?

Concept Check — click to reveal answer

In the extrinsic region, carrier concentration is approximately constant (set by doping level, \(n_0\approx N_D\)) and essentially independent of small temperature fluctuations — predictable, stable device behavior. In the freeze-out region, carrier concentration (and therefore conductivity) changes rapidly with temperature, and in the intrinsic region, doping-based control is lost entirely as thermally-generated carriers dominate — neither is desirable for reliable circuit operation.

Worked Example 4 — Identifying a Temperature Region

A doped silicon sample's carrier concentration is measured to be very close to its donor concentration \(N_D\), and does not change noticeably over a moderate temperature range around the measurement. Which temperature region is this sample in?

Solution: A flat carrier concentration approximately equal to \(N_D\), insensitive to small temperature changes, is the signature of the extrinsic temperature region — dopants are essentially fully ionized, and intrinsic generation is still negligible.

docs.title: When Doping Pushes Too Far
docs.text:
Everything in this chapter so far has assumed a non-degenerate semiconductor — one doped lightly enough that the Fermi level stays safely inside the band gap, away from either band edge, and simple statistical approximations remain valid. Push doping concentration high enough, however — comparable to or exceeding the effective density of states near the conduction (or valence) band edge — and this assumption breaks down. A degenerate semiconductor is doped so heavily that the Fermi level is pushed up to, or even past, the conduction band edge (for very heavy n-type doping) or down to, or past, the valence band edge (for very heavy p-type doping).

A useful preview (developed rigorously once Chapter 10 introduces the effective density of states \(N_C\)) is the relationship between doping and Fermi level position:

\[ E_C - E_F = k_BT\ln\!\left(\frac{N_C}{N_D}\right) \]

For silicon at room temperature, \(N_C\approx2.8\times10^{19}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\). As \(N_D\) approaches this value, \(\ln(N_C/N_D)\) shrinks toward zero, and \(E_F\) rises to meet \(E_C\); push \(N_D\) past \(N_C\) and the formula predicts \(E_F\) above \(E_C\) entirely — the hallmark of degeneracy, and a regime where this formula itself is no longer strictly valid (it assumes non-degenerate, Boltzmann-like statistics in its derivation).

docs.title: Diagram: Degenerate Semiconductor Explorer
docs.text:
How to use this MicroSim

Instructions: Drag the \(N_D\) (or switch to p-type and drag \(N_A\)) slider continuously from very light to very heavy doping and watch the Fermi level line, the doping gauge, and the non-degenerate/transition/degenerate badge move together; then adjust temperature and observe the gauge boundaries shift.

Learning objective: Predict Fermi level position from doping concentration and temperature, justify why very heavy doping invalidates the non-degenerate approximation, and recognize when a stated result is only an estimate.

What to observe: The Fermi level line stays well below \(E_C\) at low doping, and rises to meet (and cross) \(E_C\) as \(N_D\) approaches and exceeds \(N_C(T)\approx2.8\times10^{19}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\) at 300 K. Once degenerate, the line switches to a dashed "estimate," since the Boltzmann formula no longer applies.

Full MicroSim documentation →

Degenerate semiconductors are not merely a theoretical curiosity — heavily-doped regions (source/drain contacts in a MOSFET, or the emitter of a bipolar transistor) are routinely doped into the degenerate regime deliberately, since very low resistivity is often more important there than the validity of simplified carrier statistics.

Worked Example 5 — Checking for Degeneracy

A silicon sample is doped at \(N_D=5\times10^{19}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\). Using \(N_C\approx2.8\times10^{19}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\), is this sample degenerate?

Solution: Since \(N_D=5\times10^{19}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\) exceeds \(N_C\approx2.8\times10^{19}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\), the ratio \(N_C/N_D<1\), so \(\ln(N_C/N_D)<0\) and the formula predicts \(E_F\) above \(E_C\) — this sample is degenerate.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter turned Chapter 7's qualitative donor/acceptor picture into a working model of doped-semiconductor behavior. Donor doping produces n-type material (majority carrier: electrons); acceptor doping produces p-type material (majority carrier: holes). Dopant ionization is temperature-dependent, governed by the dopant's ionization energy relative to available thermal energy, and is not automatically complete. Doping concentration sets majority carrier concentration only once ionization is essentially complete. A compensated semiconductor, containing both donor and acceptor atoms, is governed by its net doping, \(N_D-N_A\) or \(N_A-N_D\). Plotting carrier concentration against temperature reveals three regions: the freeze-out regime (low T, dopants not yet ionized), the extrinsic temperature region (moderate T, carrier concentration ≈ doping level — the region most devices are designed to operate in), and the intrinsic temperature region (high T, thermal generation dominates regardless of doping). Finally, sufficiently heavy doping produces a degenerate semiconductor, where the Fermi level is pushed to or past a band edge, invalidating the simplified, non-degenerate statistics this chapter (and Chapters 9-10) otherwise rely on. Chapter 9 now develops the exact carrier-concentration statistics — the Fermi-Dirac distribution and density of states integrated together — that make every relationship in this chapter quantitatively precise.

docs.title: Key Equations
docs.text: Concept Equation Net doping (n-type if positive) \(N_{\text{net}} = N_D - N_A\) Net doping (p-type if positive) \(N_{\text{net}} = N_A - N_D\) Majority carrier concentration (extrinsic region) \(n_0\approx N_D\) (n-type), \(p_0\approx N_A\) (p-type) Simplified dopant ionization fraction \(f_{ion}(T) = \dfrac{1}{1+B\,e^{E_D/k_BT}}\) Degenerate-regime criterion (preview) \(E_C - E_F = k_BT\ln(N_C/N_D)\)

docs.text: See the Chapter 8 Glossary for full definitions of every term introduced in this chapter.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Neamen, Semiconductor Physics and Devices — direct treatment of n-type/p-type doping, freeze-out, and degenerate semiconductors
  • Sze and Ng, Physics of Semiconductor Devices — extensive treatment of compensated and heavily-doped material
  • Pierret, Semiconductor Device Fundamentals — clear derivation of the temperature-dependent ionization and carrier-freeze-out equations
  • Kittel, Introduction to Solid State Physics — background on degenerate statistics and heavily-doped semiconductors

docs.title: Worked Examples
docs.text:
Worked Example 6 — Comparing Two Dopants' Freeze-Out Behavior

Dopant A has ionization energy 30 meV; Dopant B has ionization energy 80 meV. At a fixed low temperature, which dopant will show a higher ionization fraction?

Solution: A smaller ionization energy requires less thermal energy to ionize, so Dopant A (30 meV) will have a higher ionization fraction than Dopant B (80 meV) at the same temperature — consistent with the ionization-fraction formula's dependence on \(E_D/k_BT\).

Worked Example 7 — Net Doping with Acceptors Dominant

A silicon sample has \(N_A=6\times10^{16}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\) and \(N_D=1\times10^{16}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\). Find the net doping and material type.

Solution: \(N_{\text{net}}=N_A-N_D=6\times10^{16}-1\times10^{16}=5\times10^{16}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\), positive for acceptors, so the material is net p-type with majority hole concentration approximately \(5\times10^{16}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\).

Worked Example 8 — Estimating a Region from Behavior Description

A doped sample's carrier concentration is observed to increase rapidly as temperature is raised from 20 K to 150 K, then remain nearly flat from 150 K to 400 K. Identify the two regions this describes.

Solution: The rapid increase from 20 K to 150 K describes the freeze-out regime (dopants progressively ionizing); the flat plateau from 150 K to 400 K describes the extrinsic temperature region (dopants fully ionized, intrinsic generation still negligible).

Worked Example 9 — Fully Compensated Sample

A silicon sample has \(N_D=N_A=4\times10^{16}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\) exactly. Describe its expected behavior.

Solution: Net doping is exactly zero (\(N_D-N_A=0\)), so despite containing large numbers of both donor and acceptor atoms, the sample behaves electrically as if intrinsic — its carrier concentration is governed by thermal generation alone, just like Chapter 7's pure crystal.

Worked Example 10 — Degenerate Doping in a Transistor Contact

A MOSFET's source/drain region is doped at \(N_D=1\times10^{20}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\), well above silicon's \(N_C\approx2.8\times10^{19}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\). Explain why this is done despite creating a degenerate semiconductor.

Solution: Such heavy doping is used deliberately to minimize the contact region's resistivity (more free carriers means lower resistance), which is more important for a low-resistance ohmic contact than maintaining the validity of the simplified non-degenerate carrier-statistics approximations used elsewhere in the device.

docs.title: Chapter 8 Glossary
docs.text: Terms introduced in Chapter 8 — Doping, Ionization, and Temperature Regimes. See the full site Glossary for terms across all chapters.

docs.title: Compensated Semiconductor
docs.text:
A semiconductor containing both donor and acceptor atoms simultaneously, whose majority carrier type and concentration are set by the net doping, \(N_D-N_A\) or \(N_A-N_D\), rather than either concentration alone.

Example: A sample with \(N_D=8\times10^{15}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\) and \(N_A=5\times10^{15}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\) is net n-type, with majority electron concentration approximately \(3\times10^{15}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\).

See also: N-Type Doping, P-Type Doping.

docs.title: Degenerate Semiconductor
docs.text:
A semiconductor doped so heavily that the Fermi level is pushed to or past a band edge, invalidating the non-degenerate (Boltzmann) approximation used in standard carrier-statistics equations.

Example: Silicon doped above \(N_D\approx2.8\times10^{19}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\) (its effective conduction-band density of states) becomes degenerate, as used deliberately in low-resistance transistor contacts.

See also: Doping Concentration.

docs.title: Doping Concentration
docs.text:
The number density of donor (\(N_D\)) or acceptor (\(N_A\)) atoms introduced into a semiconductor, typically expressed in atoms per cm\(^3\), which sets majority carrier concentration once dopants are fully ionized.

Example: In the extrinsic temperature region, an n-type sample doped at \(N_D=2\times10^{16}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\) has majority electron concentration \(n_0\approx2\times10^{16}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\).

See also: Extrinsic Temperature Region, Dopant Ionization.

docs.title: Dopant Ionization
docs.text:
The temperature-dependent process by which a donor releases its weakly-bound electron, or an acceptor captures a neighboring electron and releases a hole, becoming a fixed charged ion.

Example: At liquid nitrogen temperature (77 K), phosphorus donors in silicon are only partially ionized, since \(k_BT\approx6.6\) meV is much smaller than phosphorus's 45 meV ionization energy.

See also: Ionization Energy, Freeze-Out Regime.

docs.title: Extrinsic Temperature Region
docs.text:
The moderate-temperature range in which dopant atoms are essentially fully ionized but intrinsic thermal generation is still negligible, so carrier concentration levels off at approximately the doping concentration.

Example: Most semiconductor devices are designed to operate within the extrinsic temperature region, where carrier concentration is stable and set by design rather than by small temperature fluctuations.

See also: Freeze-Out Regime, Intrinsic Temperature Region.

docs.title: Freeze-Out Regime
docs.text:
The low-temperature range in which most dopant atoms have not yet ionized, so carrier concentration is well below the doping concentration and rises steeply as temperature increases.

Example: A donor-doped silicon sample cooled to 77 K shows significant freeze-out if the donor's ionization energy is much larger than \(k_BT\) at that temperature.

See also: Dopant Ionization, Extrinsic Temperature Region.

docs.title: Intrinsic Temperature Region
docs.text:
The high-temperature range in which thermally-generated intrinsic carriers exceed the fixed doping concentration, so the material behaves as if intrinsic regardless of its doping.

Example: Because intrinsic carrier concentration grows exponentially with temperature, every doped semiconductor eventually enters the intrinsic temperature region if heated enough.

See also: Extrinsic Temperature Region, Intrinsic Semiconductor.

docs.title: Ionization Energy
docs.text:
The energy required to ionize a donor or acceptor atom, well modeled by Chapter 7's hydrogenic model and typically tens of meV in silicon and germanium.

Example: A dopant with a larger ionization energy requires a higher temperature before its ionization fraction becomes significant.

See also: Dopant Ionization.

docs.title: N-Type Doping
docs.text:
Doping a semiconductor predominantly with donor atoms, making free electrons the majority carrier and holes the minority carrier.

Example: Silicon doped with phosphorus is n-type, with majority electron concentration approximately equal to the phosphorus concentration in the extrinsic region.

See also: P-Type Doping, Donor Atom.

docs.title: P-Type Doping
docs.text:
Doping a semiconductor predominantly with acceptor atoms, making holes the majority carrier and free electrons the minority carrier.

Example: Silicon doped with boron is p-type, with majority hole concentration approximately equal to the boron concentration in the extrinsic region.

See also: N-Type Doping, Acceptor Atom.

docs.title: Chapter 8 Problems - Doping, Ionization, and Temperature Regimes
End-of-Chapter Problems: Doping, Ionization, and Temperature Regimes
docs.text: Work through these problems to reinforce your understanding of doping types, ionization, and temperature regions covered in Chapter 8.

docs.title: Problem 1
docs.text:
What is the majority carrier in n-type material? In p-type material?

Show Solution

Free electrons are the majority carrier in n-type material; holes are the majority carrier in p-type material.

docs.title: Problem 2
docs.text:
What happens to a dopant's ionization fraction as temperature decreases toward absolute zero?

Show Solution

It decreases toward zero — fewer and fewer dopant atoms have enough thermal energy to ionize, the freeze-out condition.

docs.title: Problem 3
docs.text:
State the net doping formula for a compensated semiconductor.

Show Solution

\(N_{\text{net}} = N_D - N_A\) (positive means n-type; negative, in magnitude, means p-type).

docs.title: Problem 4
docs.text:
Name the three temperature regions of a doped semiconductor's carrier concentration curve, in order of increasing temperature.

Show Solution

Freeze-out regime, extrinsic temperature region, intrinsic temperature region.

docs.title: Problem 5
docs.text:
In the extrinsic temperature region, what is the approximate majority electron concentration for an n-type sample doped at \(N_D=10^{16}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\)?

Show Solution

\(n_0\approx N_D=10^{16}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\).

docs.title: Problem 6
docs.text:
What defines a degenerate semiconductor?

Show Solution

Doping so heavy that the Fermi level is pushed to or past a band edge, invalidating the non-degenerate (Boltzmann) approximation.

docs.title: Problem 7
docs.text:
A sample has \(N_D=N_A\) exactly. What is its net doping, and how does it behave electrically?

Show Solution

Net doping is zero; the sample behaves as if intrinsic despite containing both dopant species.

docs.title: Problem 8
docs.text:
State the degenerate-regime preview equation relating \(E_C-E_F\) to doping concentration.

Show Solution

\(E_C - E_F = k_BT\ln(N_C/N_D)\).

docs.title: Problem 9
docs.text:
A silicon sample is doped with arsenic (\(E_D=54\) meV) and cooled to \(T=100\) K, where \(k_BT\approx8.6\) meV. Is this sample likely well into the freeze-out regime? Explain.

Show Solution

Yes. \(E_D/k_BT\approx54/8.6\approx6.3\), meaning thermal energy is far smaller than the ionization energy — most donor atoms remain un-ionized at this temperature.

docs.title: Problem 10
docs.text:
A silicon region has \(N_D=3\times10^{16}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\) and \(N_A=1\times10^{16}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\). Find the net doping and majority carrier concentration.

Show Solution

\(N_{\text{net}}=3\times10^{16}-1\times10^{16}=2\times10^{16}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\), net n-type, with majority electron concentration approximately \(2\times10^{16}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\).

docs.title: Problem 11
docs.text:
Explain why device engineers prefer to operate circuits in the extrinsic temperature region rather than the freeze-out or intrinsic regions.

Show Solution

In the extrinsic region, carrier concentration is approximately constant (≈N_D) and insensitive to small temperature changes, giving predictable device behavior. The freeze-out and intrinsic regions both have carrier concentration that varies strongly with temperature, making device behavior unpredictable.

docs.title: Problem 12
docs.text:
Silicon's effective conduction-band density of states is \(N_C\approx2.8\times10^{19}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\). Is a sample doped at \(N_D=1\times10^{18}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\) degenerate? Justify using the preview formula.

Show Solution

Not degenerate. \(N_C/N_D=2.8\times10^{19}/1\times10^{18}=28\), so \(\ln(28)\approx3.3\), giving \(E_C-E_F\approx(0.0259)(3.3)\approx0.086\) eV — the Fermi level is still comfortably below E_C, in the non-degenerate regime.

docs.title: Problem 13
docs.text:
Two dopants have ionization energies 25 meV and 90 meV. At room temperature (\(k_BT\approx26\) meV), which is more likely to be essentially fully ionized?

Show Solution

The 25 meV dopant, since its ionization energy is comparable to or below k_BT at room temperature, while the 90 meV dopant's ionization energy is more than 3 times k_BT and would show more significant freeze-out even near room temperature.

docs.title: Problem 14
docs.text:
A doped sample's carrier concentration is measured to rise steeply, then plateau, then rise steeply again as temperature increases from very low to very high. Sketch (in words) what physical mechanism dominates in each of the three intervals.

Show Solution

First steep rise (freeze-out): progressive dopant ionization. Plateau (extrinsic): dopants essentially fully ionized, carrier concentration ≈ N_D. Second steep rise (intrinsic): thermally-generated carriers begin to exceed N_D.

docs.title: Problem 15
docs.text:
A compensated sample has \(N_A=7\times10^{16}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\) and \(N_D=2\times10^{16}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\). Find the net doping, material type, and majority carrier concentration.

Show Solution

\(N_{\text{net}}=N_A-N_D=7\times10^{16}-2\times10^{16}=5\times10^{16}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\), net p-type, majority hole concentration approximately \(5\times10^{16}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\).

docs.title: Problem 16
docs.text:
Explain why heavily-doped source/drain contacts in a MOSFET are deliberately doped into the degenerate regime.

Show Solution

Very heavy doping maximizes free carrier concentration, minimizing contact resistivity — a low-resistance ohmic contact is more important there than preserving the validity of non-degenerate carrier statistics.

docs.title: Problem 17
docs.text:
Using the simplified ionization-fraction model \(f_{ion}(T)=1/(1+B\,e^{E_D/k_BT})\) with \(B=0.02\), find the temperature at which \(f_{ion}=0.5\) for a dopant with \(E_D=0.06\) eV, using \(k_B=8.617\times10^{-5}\) eV/K.

Show Solution

Setting f_ion=0.5 requires \(B\,e^{E_D/k_BT}=1\), so \(E_D/k_BT=\ln(1/B)=\ln(50)\approx3.91\). Solving: \(T=E_D/(k_B\times3.91)=0.06/(8.617\times10^{-5}\times3.91)\approx178\) K.

docs.title: Problem 18
docs.text:
A sample is doped with \(N_D=6\times10^{16}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\) and \(N_A=6\times10^{16}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\) but is later found to have a small measurable net p-type carrier concentration of \(2\times10^{14}\ \text{cm}^{-3}\). Explain how this is possible despite the two doping concentrations appearing equal.

Show Solution

The stated concentrations may only be accurate to within measurement precision; a true, very small imbalance (N_A slightly larger than N_D by about 2×10^14 cm^-3, undetectable at the precision the two large numbers were quoted) would fully account for the observed small net p-type carrier concentration — a reminder that "equal" doping levels in practice always carry some uncertainty.

docs.title: Problem 19
docs.text:
Explain, using the degenerate-regime preview formula, why lowering temperature (at fixed \(N_D\) well below \(N_C\)) makes a sample more likely to appear degenerate by this formula, even though physically it does not become degenerate at low temperature. What does this reveal about the formula's limitations?

Show Solution

The formula \(E_C-E_F=k_BT\ln(N_C/N_D)\) has k_BT as a multiplicative prefactor, so lowering T shrinks E_C−E_F toward zero even if N_C/N_D itself does not change — misleadingly suggesting the Fermi level approaches E_C. This reveals that the formula (and the N_C value itself, which is also temperature-dependent) is only strictly valid near the temperature it was derived for, and freeze-out (not degeneracy) is the actual dominant effect at low temperature for non-degenerate doping levels — a reminder that this chapter's formulas are previews, not the full quantitative treatment Chapter 10 provides.

docs.title: Problem 20
docs.text:
A device is operated across a wide temperature range and must remain in the extrinsic temperature region throughout. Explain qualitatively how the required doping concentration \(N_D\) should be chosen relative to the maximum operating temperature, and relative to the minimum operating temperature, to keep the device extrinsic across the whole range.

Show Solution

To stay extrinsic at the maximum operating temperature, N_D must be chosen large enough that the intrinsic carrier concentration at that temperature still remains well below N_D (raising N_D pushes the intrinsic region's onset to a higher temperature). To stay extrinsic (not frozen out) at the minimum operating temperature, N_D and the dopant's ionization energy must be chosen so that the freeze-out region's upper boundary is still below the minimum operating temperature (a lower ionization-energy dopant, or a not-too-heavy doping level, helps keep freeze-out confined to temperatures below the operating range). Both constraints together bound the usable doping concentration and dopant choice for a given temperature range.

docs.title: Chapter 8 Quiz - Doping, Ionization, and Temperature Regimes
Quiz: Doping, Ionization, and Temperature Regimes
docs.text:
Test your understanding of doping types, ionization, and temperature regions covered in Chapter 8 with these 20 questions.

Question 1

What is the majority carrier in n-type material?

  1. Holes
  2. Free electrons
  3. Protons
  4. Neutrons
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

N-type material is doped with donors, so free electrons are its majority carrier.

Concept Tested: N-Type Doping

Question 2

What is the majority carrier in p-type material?

  1. Free electrons
  2. Holes
  3. Protons
  4. Photons
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

P-type material is doped with acceptors, so holes are its majority carrier.

Concept Tested: P-Type Doping

Question 3

What does "dopant ionization" refer to?

  1. The permanent destruction of a dopant atom
  2. The temperature-dependent process of a donor releasing its electron or an acceptor capturing one
  3. A process that only happens at absolute zero
  4. Breaking a covalent bond in pure silicon
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Dopant ionization is the temperature-dependent release of a donor's electron (or capture of an electron by an acceptor), not related to breaking a covalent bond.

Concept Tested: Dopant Ionization

Question 4

What quantity determines how much thermal energy a dopant needs before it substantially ionizes?

  1. Its ionization energy
  2. Its atomic radius
  3. Its melting point
  4. Its color
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

A dopant's ionization energy, compared to available thermal energy k_BT, determines its ionization fraction at a given temperature.

Concept Tested: Ionization Energy

Question 5

In the extrinsic temperature region, what does majority carrier concentration approximately equal?

  1. The intrinsic carrier concentration
  2. The doping concentration
  3. Zero
  4. The silicon atomic density
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

In the extrinsic region, dopants are essentially fully ionized, so majority carrier concentration ≈ doping concentration.

Concept Tested: Doping Concentration

Question 6

What determines majority carrier type in a compensated semiconductor?

  1. N_D alone
  2. N_A alone
  3. The net doping, N_D − N_A
  4. The crystal's color
Show Answer

Correct Answer: C

Because donor electrons and acceptor holes can recombine, only the net doping, N_D − N_A, determines the majority carrier type and concentration.

Concept Tested: Compensated Semiconductor

Question 7

A sample has N_D = N_A exactly. How does it behave?

  1. As a metal
  2. As if intrinsic
  3. As a pure insulator
  4. It has no electrons at all
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

With net doping exactly zero, the sample behaves electrically as if intrinsic, despite containing both dopant species.

Concept Tested: Compensated Semiconductor

Question 8

What happens to carrier concentration in the freeze-out regime as temperature increases?

  1. It decreases
  2. It rises steeply as dopants progressively ionize
  3. It stays exactly constant
  4. It becomes negative
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

As temperature rises through the freeze-out regime, more dopant atoms gain enough thermal energy to ionize, so carrier concentration rises steeply.

Concept Tested: Freeze-Out Regime

Question 9

Why is the extrinsic temperature region generally preferred for device operation?

  1. Carrier concentration is approximately constant and set by design, not by small temperature changes
  2. It is the coldest possible temperature
  3. It is the only region where atoms exist
  4. Devices cannot operate in any other region at all
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

In the extrinsic region, carrier concentration ≈ N_D and is stable against small temperature fluctuations, giving predictable device behavior.

Concept Tested: Extrinsic Temperature Region

Question 10

Why does carrier concentration eventually rise again at very high temperature, regardless of doping?

  1. Donor atoms multiply
  2. Thermally-generated intrinsic carriers eventually exceed the doping concentration
  3. The band gap becomes infinite
  4. It does not rise again
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Intrinsic carrier concentration grows exponentially with temperature and eventually exceeds any fixed doping concentration, entering the intrinsic temperature region.

Concept Tested: Intrinsic Temperature Region

Question 11

What defines a degenerate semiconductor?

  1. A material with no dopants at all
  2. Doping so heavy the Fermi level is pushed to or past a band edge
  3. A material with an infinite band gap
  4. A material at absolute zero only
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

A degenerate semiconductor is doped heavily enough that the Fermi level reaches or crosses a band edge, invalidating non-degenerate statistics.

Concept Tested: Degenerate Semiconductor

Question 12

Approximately what is silicon's effective conduction-band density of states, N_C, at room temperature?

  1. 2.8×10^19 cm^-3
  2. 5×10^22 cm^-3
  3. 10^10 cm^-3
  4. 1.12 eV
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

Silicon's N_C is approximately 2.8×10^19 cm^-3 at room temperature; doping near or above this value produces a degenerate semiconductor.

Concept Tested: Degenerate Semiconductor

Question 13

Why are heavily-doped MOSFET source/drain contacts deliberately made degenerate?

  1. To maximize resistivity
  2. To minimize resistivity for a good low-resistance contact
  3. Degeneracy is unavoidable and serves no purpose
  4. To eliminate all carriers
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Very heavy doping maximizes carrier concentration, minimizing contact resistivity — more important there than preserving non-degenerate statistics.

Concept Tested: Degenerate Semiconductor

Question 14

A dopant with a larger ionization energy, compared to one with a smaller ionization energy, will show significant ionization at what kind of temperature?

  1. A lower temperature
  2. A higher temperature
  3. Exactly the same temperature always
  4. Ionization energy has no effect on this
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

A larger ionization energy requires more thermal energy (a higher temperature) before the ionization fraction becomes significant.

Concept Tested: Ionization Energy

Question 15

Increasing N_D in the freeze-out/extrinsic/intrinsic carrier-concentration curve does what to the extrinsic plateau?

  1. Lowers it
  2. Raises it
  3. Has no effect on it
  4. Removes it entirely
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Since the extrinsic plateau height is set by N_D itself, increasing N_D raises the plateau.

Concept Tested: Doping Concentration

Question 16

A silicon sample has N_A = 6×10^16 cm^-3 and N_D = 1×10^16 cm^-3. What is the material type?

  1. n-type
  2. p-type
  3. Intrinsic
  4. Degenerate metal
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Since N_A > N_D, net doping is positive for acceptors, making this p-type material.

Concept Tested: P-Type Doping

Question 17

What minority carrier exists in n-type material?

  1. Free electrons
  2. Holes
  3. Donor ions
  4. Photons
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Holes are the minority carrier in n-type material, present in small numbers relative to the majority electrons.

Concept Tested: N-Type Doping

Question 18

Why does complete ionization become a good approximation near and above room temperature for typical silicon dopants?

  1. Because measured donor/acceptor ionization energies (tens of meV) are comparable to room-temperature thermal energy (~26 meV)
  2. Because dopant atoms disappear above 0°C
  3. Because silicon melts at room temperature
  4. It is not actually a good approximation at room temperature
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

Because typical ionization energies are only a few times k_BT at room temperature (or less), essentially all dopants are ionized at and above room temperature.

Concept Tested: Dopant Ionization

Question 19

What happens to the freeze-out region's temperature extent if a dopant with a larger ionization energy is used (all else equal)?

  1. The freeze-out region shrinks to zero
  2. The freeze-out region stretches to higher temperature
  3. The freeze-out region disappears
  4. There is no freeze-out region for any dopant
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

A larger ionization energy means more thermal energy (higher temperature) is needed to ionize the dopant, stretching the freeze-out region to higher temperature.

Concept Tested: Freeze-Out Regime

Question 20

Which chapter develops the exact, quantitative carrier-concentration equations that make this chapter's relationships precise?

  1. Chapter 9
  2. Chapter 3
  3. Chapter 1
  4. No later chapter builds on this one
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

Chapter 9, "Carrier Concentration Statistics," develops the exact Fermi-Dirac and density-of-states equations that make this chapter's relationships quantitatively precise.

Concept Tested: Doping Concentration
