docs.title: Coulomb's Law Force and Field Explorer
docs.text:
Coulomb's Law Force and Field Explorer

← Back to Chapter 1: Physics and Math Foundations

Description

This MicroSim lets students adjust two point charges (\(q_1\), \(q_2\)) and their separation (\(r\)) and immediately see the resulting electrostatic force \(F\), the electric field \(E\) and potential \(V\) that \(q_1\) creates at \(q_2\)'s location, and the electrostatic potential energy \(U\) of the pair — all computed from real SI values using \(k=8.99\times10^9\ \text{N·m}^2/\text{C}^2\).

Key Features

  • ● Three independent sliders for \(q_1\), \(q_2\) (−5 to +5 nC), and separation \(r\) (0.2 to 5 nm)
  • ● Live numeric readouts of force, field, potential, and energy in scientific notation
  • ● Log-scaled force arrows so both very small and very large forces remain visible on screen
  • ● Reset button returning to the default \(q_1=+2\) nC, \(q_2=-1\) nC, \(r=1\) nm
How to Use
  1. Drag the \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) sliders to change charge magnitude and sign
  2. Drag the \(r\) slider to change separation and watch \(F\) change much faster than \(E\) or \(V\)
  3. Read the numeric panel to see the exact computed values in SI units
  4. Click Reset to return to the default configuration
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply (L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Calculate

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Apply Coulomb's Law to compute the force between two point charges
  • ✓ Apply the point-charge field and potential equations to compute \(E\) and \(V\)
  • ✓ Verify, by direct manipulation, that force falls off faster with distance (\(1/r^2\)) than potential does (\(1/r\))
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the boxed Coulomb's Law, field, and potential equations from the chapter
  • ● Ask students to predict what happens to \(F\) if \(r\) is doubled
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Set \(q_1=q_2=2\) nC and record \(F\), \(E\), \(V\), \(U\) at \(r=1\) nm
  2. Double \(r\) to 2 nm and compare the new readouts against the prediction (\(F\) should drop to 1/4, \(V\) to 1/2)
  3. Flip the sign of \(q_2\) and observe the arrows reverse direction and \(U\) become negative
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Compare results with Worked Example 9 in the chapter
  • ● Discuss why this distinction matters for the depletion-region field in Chapter 14
References
  • ● Coulomb's Law — Wikipedia

docs.title: Crystal Structure Explorer
docs.text:
Crystal Structure Explorer

← Back to Chapter 3: Crystal Lattices and Structures

Description

This MicroSim renders a fully rotatable, pannable, and zoomable 3D model of one conventional unit cell for each of the nine crystal structures most important to solid-state and semiconductor physics: Simple Cubic (SC), Body-Centered Cubic (BCC), Face-Centered Cubic (FCC), Hexagonal Close-Packed (HCP), Diamond Cubic, Zinc Blende, Rock Salt (NaCl), Cesium Chloride (CsCl), and Wurtzite. A dropdown switches between structures; atoms are drawn at their correct fractional positions with correct sharing/coordination, compound structures use a distinct color per species with a legend, and a live readout panel reports crystal system, Bravais lattice and basis, atoms per conventional cell, coordination number, nearest-neighbor distance, atomic packing factor, example materials, and semiconductor relevance for whichever structure is selected.

This tool was expanded from an earlier "Cubic Lattice Explorer" that covered only SC, BCC, and FCC. Because HCP and the two hexagonal-family structures (Wurtzite) are not cubic, the tool and its title were generalized to Crystal Structure Explorer to accurately describe its full scope.

Key Features

  • ● Nine structures in one tool: SC, BCC, FCC, HCP, Diamond Cubic, Zinc Blende, Rock Salt, CsCl, and Wurtzite
  • ● Free 3D orbit, pan, and zoom via p5.js \(\texttt{orbitControl()}\) — left-drag to rotate, right-drag to pan, scroll to zoom
  • ● Color-coded species with a legend for every compound structure (Zinc Blende, Rock Salt, CsCl, Wurtzite)
  • ● Toggleable atom labels, unit-cell edges, nearest-neighbor bonds, and primitive-vs-conventional cell so students can isolate exactly one variable at a time
  • ● Adjustable atom size and a Reset Camera button
  • ● Miller-index plane (h k l) and direction [u v w] overlay for the six cubic structures
  • ● Fullscreen mode for closer inspection on smaller screens
  • ● Live readout panel reporting crystal system, Bravais lattice/basis, atoms per cell, coordination number, nearest-neighbor distance, packing factor, examples, and semiconductor relevance
Structure Reference Table

All lattice-parameter relationships below use \(a\) for the cubic lattice constant and \(c\) for the hexagonal out-of-plane constant (ideal \(c/a=\sqrt{8/3}\approx1.633\)).

Structure Crystal system Bravais lattice + basis Atoms/cell Coord. number Nearest-neighbor distance Packing factor Example materials Simple Cubic (SC) Cubic Simple cubic (P); 1 atom at (0,0,0) 1 6 \(a\) 0.524 Polonium Body-Centered Cubic (BCC) Cubic Body-centered cubic (I); (0,0,0) + (½,½,½) 2 8 \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}a\) 0.680 α-Fe, Cr, W, Na Face-Centered Cubic (FCC) Cubic Face-centered cubic (F); (0,0,0) + 3 face centers 4 12 \(\tfrac{a}{\sqrt2}\) 0.740 Al, Cu, Au, Ag Hexagonal Close-Packed (HCP) Hexagonal Simple hexagonal + 2-atom basis, ABAB stacking 6 12 \(a\) 0.740 Mg, Zn, Ti, Co, Be Diamond Cubic Cubic FCC + 2-atom basis (0,0,0), (¼,¼,¼), same element 8 4 \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}a\) 0.340 Si (a=0.543 nm), Ge (a=0.566 nm), C Zinc Blende Cubic FCC + 2-atom basis (0,0,0), (¼,¼,¼), two species 8 4 \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}a\) varies with ionic/atomic radii GaAs (a=0.565 nm), GaP, InP, InAs, ZnS Rock Salt (NaCl) Cubic Two interpenetrating FCC lattices offset by (½,0,0)a 8 6 \(\tfrac{a}{2}\) varies with ionic radii NaCl, MgO Cesium Chloride (CsCl) Cubic Simple cubic (P) + 2-atom basis (0,0,0), (½,½,½), two species 2 8 \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}a\) varies with ionic radii CsCl, CsBr, CsI Wurtzite Hexagonal Two HCP-type sublattices offset along c by u (ideal u=3/8), two species 12 4 \(u\cdot c \approx 0.612a\) varies with ionic/atomic radii GaN, AlN, ZnO, CdS

Special Focus: Diamond Cubic and Zinc Blende

These two structures are geometrically identical — both are built from two interpenetrating FCC sublattices offset by \((1/4,1/4,1/4)a\) along the body diagonal, giving every atom exactly 4 nearest neighbors arranged tetrahedrally (coordination number 4, far lower than the 12 of a simple FCC lattice). The only difference is chemistry:

  • ● Diamond Cubic places the same element on both sublattices. Silicon and germanium — the two workhorse elemental semiconductors — both crystallize this way, with covalent Si–Si or Ge–Ge bonds arranged tetrahedrally.
  • ● Zinc Blende places two different elements, one per sublattice. GaAs is the canonical example — most III–V compound semiconductors (GaAs, GaP, InP, InAs) used in LEDs, laser diodes, solar cells, and high-frequency transistors adopt this structure. The two-species arrangement breaks the inversion symmetry that pure Diamond Cubic has, which is why compound semiconductors can be piezoelectric while silicon and germanium cannot.
How to Use
  1. Choose a structure from the Crystal structure dropdown (9 options, grouped from simplest to most complex)
  2. Left-click and drag to orbit the structure; right-click and drag to pan; scroll or pinch to zoom
  3. Toggle atom labels, unit-cell edges, nearest-neighbor bonds, and the primitive-cell overlay to isolate what you want to inspect
  4. Enable the plane/direction overlay and enter Miller indices (h k l) or a direction [u v w] to see crystallographic planes and directions for the cubic structures
  5. Use Reset Camera to return to the default view, or the fullscreen button (top-right of the canvas) to enlarge the whole tool
  6. Read the panel below the canvas for crystal system, Bravais lattice/basis, atoms per cell, coordination number, nearest-neighbor distance, packing factor, examples, and semiconductor relevance
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand / Apply / Analyze (L2-L4)  |  Bloom Verb: Identify, Calculate, Compare, Explain

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Identify the atom positions that define all nine major crystal structures used in solid-state and semiconductor physics
  • ✓ Calculate atoms per unit cell using corner, face, edge, and body-center sharing fractions
  • ✓ Compare coordination number and atomic packing factor across cubic, hexagonal, and compound structures
  • ✓ Explain why Silicon and Germanium adopt Diamond Cubic while III–V compounds such as GaAs adopt the geometrically identical Zinc Blende structure
  • ✓ Distinguish a true Bravais lattice from a lattice-plus-basis description, using CsCl (Simple Cubic + 2-atom basis, not BCC) as a concrete counterexample
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review unit cell, lattice constant, basis, and coordination number from the chapter
  • ● Ask students to predict which structures pack atoms most and least efficiently
During the Simulation (15 minutes)
  1. Cycle through SC → BCC → FCC → HCP and record atoms/cell, coordination number, and packing factor for each
  2. Switch to Diamond Cubic, enable bonds, and count the 4 tetrahedral bonds leaving an interior atom; compare to FCC's coordination of 12
  3. Switch to Zinc Blende and observe that every bond connects a blue and an orange atom, never two of the same color
  4. Compare Rock Salt (CN=6, octahedral) and CsCl (CN=8, cubic) to Zinc Blende (CN=4, tetrahedral) to see how coordination geometry differs by structure
  5. Switch to Wurtzite (GaN) and compare its two-sublattice hexagonal geometry to plain HCP
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Have students derive the packing-fraction formulas for SC, BCC, and FCC on paper and compare to the readout values
  • ● Discuss why silicon (Diamond Cubic) and GaAs (Zinc Blende) share identical geometry but different electrical and optical properties, previewing the covalent-bonding discussion in Chapter 4

docs.title: de Broglie Wavelength Explorer
docs.text:
de Broglie Wavelength Explorer

← Back to Chapter 2: Quantum Mechanics Foundations

Description

This MicroSim lets students choose an object — electron, proton, neutron, baseball, bowling ball, or a custom mass — and a velocity, then computes its de Broglie wavelength \(\lambda = h/(mv)\) using \(h = 6.626\times10^{-34}\) J·s. A log-scale ruler plots the computed wavelength alongside reference lengths (atomic diameter, visible-light wavelength, red blood cell diameter) to make it visually obvious that matter waves only matter at quantum scales.

Key Features

  • ● Object dropdown with electron, proton, neutron, baseball, bowling ball, and custom mass presets
  • ● Custom mass slider on a log10 scale spanning subatomic to macroscopic masses
  • ● Velocity slider from 0 to \(10^7\) m/s (non-relativistic range)
  • ● Log-scale ruler comparing the computed wavelength to atomic diameter, visible light, and a red blood cell
  • ● Three preset buttons for a fast electron, a thermal neutron, and a thrown baseball
How to Use
  1. Choose an object from the dropdown, or select "Custom" to unlock the mass slider
  2. Drag the velocity slider and watch the wavelength readout and ruler marker respond
  3. Click a preset button to jump to a worked-example configuration
  4. Compare the red marker to the green reference lines to judge whether the wavelength is quantum-scale or immeasurably small
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply (L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Calculate

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Apply \(\lambda = h/(mv)\) to compute the de Broglie wavelength of any object
  • ✓ Compare wavelengths across many orders of magnitude using a log-scale ruler
  • ✓ Explain why matter waves are observable for electrons and neutrons but not for macroscopic objects
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the boxed de Broglie relation \(\lambda = h/(mv)\) from the chapter
  • ● Ask students to predict whether a thrown baseball has a measurable wavelength
During the Simulation (10 minutes)

  3. Click "Baseball" and confirm the marker falls completely off the left edge of the ruler
After the Simulation (5 minutes)

  • ● Connect this scale argument to why quantum effects dominate carrier transport in semiconductors later in the course

Degenerate Semiconductor Explorer

Description

This MicroSim computes \(E_C-E_F=k_BT\ln(N_C(T)/N_D)\) (n-type) or \(E_F-E_V=k_BT\ln(N_V(T)/N_A)\) (p-type) and draws the resulting Fermi level position on a schematic band diagram (\(E_C\), \(E_i\), \(E_V\)) as the doping and temperature sliders move. A live doping gauge shows three zones — non-degenerate, transition, and degenerate — with boundaries that shift correctly as temperature changes \(N_C(T)\) or \(N_V(T)\). Once the formula predicts \(E_F\) at or past a band edge, the diagram switches to an explicitly-labeled dashed "estimate" line and the explanation text states plainly that the non-degenerate Boltzmann approximation no longer applies.

Key Features

  • ● n-type and p-type modes, each with its own band-edge and effective-density-of-states formula
  • ● Temperature control that correctly scales N_C(T)/N_V(T) as T^1.5
  • ● Live non-degenerate / transition / degenerate doping gauge with a moving marker
  • ● Explicit approximation-validity warning once the Boltzmann formula breaks down
  • ● Responsive canvas that resizes with the browser window, with fullscreen support

docs.title: Density of States and Fermi Level Explorer
docs.text:
Density of States and Fermi Level Explorer

← Back to Chapter 6: Band Structure and the Fermi Level

Description

This MicroSim draws a valence-like density of states \(g_v(E)\propto\sqrt{E_v-E}\) and a conduction-like density of states \(g_c(E)\propto\sqrt{E-E_c}\) side by side with a matching band diagram, for six presets: Metal and Semimetal (where the two bands overlap in energy) and Intrinsic, n-type, and p-type Semiconductor and Insulator (where they are separated by a real gap of different sizes, and where the Fermi level EF shifts for doped semiconductors). Both panels are shaded by the Fermi-Dirac occupation probability \(f(E)=1/[1+\exp((E-E_F)/k_BT)]\), so changing the Temperature T (K) control visibly smears the sharp T=0 occupied/empty boundary near the dashed EF line. A legend and a numeric readout (kT, Eg, EF, f(Ec), f(Ev)) make every quantity explicit.

Key Features

  • ● Six presets: Metal, Insulator, Semimetal, Intrinsic/n-type/p-type Semiconductor, all built from the same underlying model
  • ● Clearly separated band-diagram and density-of-states panels sharing the same energy axis, with a divider line
  • ● Live Fermi-Dirac shading with a legend distinguishing occupied vs. unoccupied states
  • ● Temperature T (K) control with 0 K / 77 K / 300 K / 600 K presets, plus a fine slider
  • ● Numeric readout of kT, Eg, EF, f(Ec), and f(Ev)
  • ● Responsive canvas that resizes with the browser window, with fullscreen support
How to Use
  1. Select "Insulator" and confirm EF sits in a wide pale-gray (empty) gap between the green and purple bands
  2. Switch to "Intrinsic Semiconductor" and compare the much narrower gap, with EF still inside it
  3. Switch to "n-type" and "p-type" and watch EF shift toward Ec and Ev respectively
  4. Switch to "Metal" then "Semimetal", and step through the Temperature presets, to compare density of states and thermal smearing at EF
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand / Analyze (L2-L4)  |  Bloom Verb: Interpret, Compare, Classify

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Interpret a density-of-states curve and identify where it is zero versus nonzero
  • ✓ Compare Fermi-level position relative to the bands across metal, insulator, semimetal, and intrinsic/n-type/p-type semiconductor presets
  • ✓ Classify a material from its band-structure and Fermi-level picture alone
  • ✓ Connect temperature T (K) to thermal smearing of the Fermi-Dirac occupation boundary

Diamond / Zincblende Structure Explorer

← Back to Chapter 3: Crystal Lattices and Structures

Description

This MicroSim renders the diamond-cubic conventional unit cell as two interpenetrating Face-Centered Cubic sublattices — one at the corners and face centers, the other offset by \((\tfrac14,\tfrac14,\tfrac14)a\) along the body diagonal — connected by the four tetrahedral bonds that give every atom coordination number 4. Students click and drag to orbit the structure and toggle between Diamond mode (a single element, such as silicon) and Zincblende mode (two elements, such as gallium and arsenide, distinguished by color).

Key Features

  • ● Free 3D rotation via p5.js \(\texttt{orbitControl()}\) — click-drag to spin, scroll to zoom
  • ● Diamond / Zincblende toggle switching between single-species and two-species coloring with a legend
  • ● 16 tetrahedral bonds drawn between each of the 4 interior atoms and its 4 nearest neighbors

  • ✓ Distinguish diamond (single-species) from zincblende (two-species) structures despite identical geometry
  • ✓ Explain why tetrahedral bonding gives coordination number 4, lower than close-packed cubic structures

docs.title: Direct vs. Indirect Bandgap E-k Explorer
docs.text:
Direct vs. Indirect Bandgap E-k Explorer

← Back to Chapter 6: Band Structure and the Fermi Level

Description

This MicroSim plots simplified valence- and conduction-band parabolas on an E-k diagram, \(E_v(k)=-B_vk^2\) and \(E_c(k)=E_g+a(k-k_0)^2\), for three material presets: direct-gap GaAs (\(k_0=0\)) and indirect-gap Si and Ge (\(k_0\neq0\)). A transition arrow shows either a vertical, photon-only jump at \(k=0\), or a diagonal path split into a vertical photon segment (energy \(E_g\)) and a horizontal phonon segment (momentum \(k_0\)) that together reach the true conduction-band minimum. An effective-mass slider adjusts the conduction band's curvature directly, making the inverse relationship between curvature and effective mass visible.

Key Features

  • ● Three material presets: GaAs (direct), Si (indirect), Ge (indirect), with realistic band gaps
  • ● Switchable transition arrow: vertical (photon only) vs. diagonal (phonon-assisted)
  • ● Adjustable effective mass directly controls conduction-band curvature
  • ● Labeled band extrema mark the valence-band maximum and conduction-band minimum, with a measured Eg bracket
  • ● Color-coded photon (orange) vs. phonon (dashed teal) transition segments
  • ● Electron vs. hole effective mass readout compares conduction- and valence-band curvature side by side
  • ● Responsive canvas that resizes with the browser window, with fullscreen support
How to Use
  1. Select "GaAs (Direct)" with "Vertical (photon only)" transition and confirm the arrow lands exactly on the conduction-band minimum
  2. Switch to "Si (Indirect)" and see the same vertical arrow now miss the true minimum, which has shifted to a nonzero k₀
  3. Change Transition to "Diagonal (phonon-assisted)" and confirm the path now reaches the true minimum via a photon segment plus a phonon segment
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand / Analyze (L2-L4)  |  Bloom Verb: Identify, Compare, Analyze

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Identify direct vs. indirect band gaps directly from an E-k diagram
  • ✓ Explain why a photon-only transition can reach the conduction-band minimum only when k₀ = 0
  • ✓ Connect conduction-band curvature to effective mass, and compare curvature across materials

Drift Current Density Explorer

← Back to Chapter 11: Drift Current and Carrier Mobility

Description

This MicroSim computes \(J_n=qn_0\mu_nE\) and \(J_p=qp_0\mu_pE\) in real units (A/cm²) for a chosen material, doping level, temperature, and applied field — combining Chapter 9-10's exact carrier concentration equations with Chapter 11's Matthiessen's-rule mobility model. A log-scale bar chart and a plain-language summary make the majority-carrier dominance the mass action law predicts directly visible, rather than something to take on faith from a single worked example.

Key Features

  • ● Real physical units throughout (cm⁻³, cm²/V·s, V/cm, A/cm²) instead of arbitrary scales

docs.title: Electric Field and Flux Explorer
docs.text:
Electric Field and Flux Explorer

← Back to Chapter 1: Physics and Math Foundations

Description

This MicroSim shows the radial electric field of a point charge together with a small flat test surface placed a fixed distance away. A slider tilts the surface's normal vector relative to the field, and a live readout shows the electric field magnitude, the surface area, and the resulting flux \(\Phi_E = EA\cos\theta\) — including the special cases of maximum flux (\(\theta=0°\), normal aligned with the field) and zero flux (\(\theta=90°\), surface parallel to the field).

Key Features

  • ● Charge slider (−5 to +5 nC) that reverses the field direction and the color of the radiating arrows
  • ● Distance slider moving the test surface closer to or farther from the charge
  • ● Angle slider (0–90°) tilting the surface's normal vector relative to the field
  • ● Live numeric readout of \(E\), \(\cos\theta\), and \(\Phi_E\)
How to Use
  1. Set the angle slider to 0° and note the flux is at its maximum (normal aligned with the field)
  2. Slide the angle to 90° and note the flux drops to exactly zero
  3. Change the distance slider and observe that \(E\) changes but \(\Phi_E\) still scales the same way with \(\cos\theta\)
  4. Flip the charge sign to see the field arrows reverse direction
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply (L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Calculate

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Compute the electric field of a point charge at a given distance
  • ✓ Apply \(\Phi_E = EA\cos\theta\) to compute electric flux through a flat surface
  • ✓ Explain why flux is maximized when a surface is perpendicular to the field and zero when parallel to it
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the definition of electric flux from the chapter
  • ● Ask students to predict the flux at θ=45°
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Sweep the angle slider from 0° to 90° and record the flux at 0°, 45°, and 90°
  2. Verify the 45° value matches \(E \cdot A \cdot \cos(45°)\) computed by hand
  3. Move the surface closer to the charge and note how much faster \(E\) grows than a linear change
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Preview the next MicroSim (Gauss's Law Explorer), which shows what happens when a surface completely encloses the charge
  • ● Discuss why a solar cell's tilt angle relative to the sun affects the light flux it captures, as a real-world analogy
References

Electron Configuration Explorer

  2. Press "Na" and "Cl" and compare their valence electron counts (1 and 7) to silicon's 4

docs.title: Energy Band Formation Explorer
docs.text:
Energy Band Formation Explorer

← Back to Chapter 5: Quantum Mechanics of Periodic Crystals

Description

This MicroSim visualizes the physical origin of band formation, before the Kronig-Penney model formalizes it mathematically. Every isolated atom has the same sharp, discrete energy levels. As N identical atoms are brought together, their wavefunctions begin to overlap, and each level splits into N closely-spaced sub-levels — modeled here as a simple finite tight-binding spectrum, \(E_j = E_0 \pm t(d)\cos\!\big(\tfrac{\pi(j+1)}{N+1}\big)\), where the coupling strength \(t(d)\) grows as the interatomic spacing \(d\) shrinks. A "fan diagram" traces all N split states continuously as spacing varies, so you can watch a single sharp line (isolated atoms) spread into a band of N discrete states, and — for large N — into what looks like a continuous band exactly like the ones the Kronig-Penney model produces.

Key Features

  • ● Schematic atom row that visibly moves together as the spacing slider decreases
  • ● Continuous fan diagram tracing every split state across the full spacing range
  • ● Adjustable atom count N (2-40) showing individually-countable levels vs. a quasi-continuous band
  • ● Live numerical readout of each band's width and the gap between them
  • ● Valence/conduction band labels at the equilibrium-spacing end, connecting directly to this chapter's terminology
  • ● Responsive canvas that resizes with the browser window
How to Use
  1. Set N to a small value like 3, and drag the spacing slider from large to small, counting the discrete split levels
  2. Increase N to 40 and confirm the same splitting now looks like two continuous shaded bands
  3. Compare the "Gap between bands" readout to each band's width as you change the spacing
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand / Apply (L2-L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Explain, Predict, Compare

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Explain why isolated atoms have sharp discrete levels while atoms in a crystal have energy bands
  • ✓ Predict how decreasing interatomic spacing changes a band's width
  • ✓ Compare a small-N discrete spectrum to a large-N quasi-continuous band and connect the large-N limit to a real crystal
References
  • ● Electronic Band Structure — Wikipedia
  • ● Tight-Binding Model — Wikipedia
  • ● Bloch's Theorem — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 5: Quantum Mechanics of Periodic Crystals — this textbook

docs.title: Carrier Concentration and Charge Neutrality Explorer
docs.text:
Carrier Concentration and Charge Neutrality Explorer

← Back to Chapter 10: Fermi Level Position and Carrier Equations

Description

This MicroSim computes electron and hole concentration exactly, by solving the mass action law and charge neutrality condition together: \(n_0=\big[(N_D-N_A)+\sqrt{(N_D-N_A)^2+4n_i^2}\big]/2\), with \(p_0=n_i^2/n_0\). A charge-balance visualization shows both equations being satisfied simultaneously — a "positive charge" tower (\(p_0+N_D\)) and a "negative charge" tower (\(n_0+N_A\)) that always reach the same height — while the info panel compares the exact \(n_0\) to the common shortcut \(n_0\approx N_D-N_A\) and reports the percent difference. Presets jump directly to intrinsic, n-type, p-type, compensated, and nearly-compensated doping.

Key Features

  • ● Charge-balance visualization of both the mass action law and charge neutrality condition together
  • ● Five doping presets: intrinsic, n-type, p-type, compensated, nearly compensated
  • ● Exact-vs-approximate comparison with a live percent-difference readout
  • ● Majority/minority carrier labels that update live
  • ● Responsive canvas that resizes with the browser window, with fullscreen support
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply / Analyze (L3-L4)  |  Bloom Verb: Calculate, Verify, Compare

  • ✓ Verify that the extrinsic and intrinsic approximations are limiting cases of one exact formula

Exact vs. Approximate Carrier Solution Explorer

A selectable tolerance (1%, 5%, or 10%) shades the region where the approximation is trustworthy, and a live crossover reading reports the smallest doping level where it first meets that tolerance — teaching students not just the formulas, but when they may safely be simplified.

Key Features

  • ● Error-vs-doping curve spanning 10⁶ to 10¹⁹ cm⁻³ on a log axis
  • ● Selectable tolerance (1%/5%/10%) with a live crossover-point readout
  • ● Independent N_A control showing how compensation shifts the whole curve
  • ● Si / Ge / GaAs and temperature control showing the crossover point depends on nᵢ, not on N_D alone

docs.title: Excess Carrier Generation and Recombination Explorer
docs.text:
Excess Carrier Generation and Recombination Explorer

← Back to Chapter 13: Non-Equilibrium Carriers and Recombination

Description

This MicroSim plots excess minority carrier concentration \(\Delta n(t)\) and \(\Delta p(t)\) under student-controlled generation: a real Start/Stop toggle lets you turn generation on (approach toward a steady state \(\Delta n_{ss}=G\tau\), derived directly from the generation rate \(G\) and lifetime \(\tau\)) or off (exponential decay, \(\Delta n(t)=\Delta n(T_{on})e^{-(t-T_{on})/\tau}\), starting from whenever you choose to stop generation). One full lifetime is marked directly on the decay curve. A movable time marker reads off the instantaneous excess concentration, recombination rate \(R=\Delta n/\tau\), and a preview of the injection-level ratio \(\Delta n/N\) covered in the next section.

Key Features

  • ● Real Start/Stop generation toggle, not a fixed on-time
  • ● G (generation rate) slider — Δn_ss = G·τ is derived forward, not assumed
  • ● Δn(t) and Δp(t) plotted together, showing charge-neutrality equality directly
  • ● One lifetime τ marked directly on the decay curve
  • ● Working optical/thermal generation presets that actually change G
  • ● Responsive canvas that resizes with the browser window
Learning Objectives

An independent Fermi level slider translates the curve left and right, while a Temperature T (K) control (with 0 K / 77 K / 300 K / 600 K presets) changes how gradually the curve transitions. A red marker always shows that the curve crosses exactly f = 0.5 at E = EF, and a faint gray step-function overlay shows the T→0 limiting case for direct comparison.

Key Features

  • ● Independent EF and Temperature controls, so translation and steepness effects can be studied separately
  • ● Temperature presets: 0 K, 77 K (liquid nitrogen), 300 K (room temperature), 600 K

  • ● T→0 step-function reference shown faintly for direct visual comparison

The info panel reports \(E_F\) relative to \(E_C\), \(E_V\), and \(E_i\) simultaneously, along with \(n_0\), \(p_0\), and \(n_i\), and a live badge warns when heavy doping pushes \(E_F\) into the degenerate regime where this chapter's non-degenerate formulas no longer apply.

An electric field slider adds a drift current contribution; J_diffusion, J_drift, and J_total are plotted together across the full bar, and a "Snap to cancellation field" button finds the exact field where drift and diffusion cancel at the marker.

← Back to Chapter 2: Quantum Mechanics Foundations

Description

This MicroSim numerically solves for the bound-state energies of a symmetric finite square well of adjustable width \(L\) and depth \(V_0\), using bisection root-finding on the standard even/odd transcendental matching equations. It plots the well, a dashed energy level for every bound state found, and the selected eigenfunction — clearly showing the wavefunction decaying smoothly into the classically forbidden region outside the well, rather than dropping to exactly zero as it does in the idealized infinite well of Particle in a Box.

Key Features

  • ● Exact bisection solver for finite-well bound states, not an approximation
  • ● Bound-state dropdown that updates automatically as L and V₀ change the available state count
  • ● Infinite-well overlay toggle for a direct side-by-side wavefunction comparison
  • ● Live energy-level ladder with parity (even/odd) labels for every bound state
How to Use
  1. Drag V₀ from minimum to maximum and watch the "Bound states found" count grow
  2. Select each bound state from the dropdown and count its internal nodes
  3. Check "Compare to infinite well" to see the dashed curve forced to zero at the walls versus the solid curve that penetrates them
  4. Adjust L and observe how a wider well packs energy levels more closely together
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply / Analyze (L3-L4)  |  Bloom Verb: Calculate, Contrast

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Calculate how the number of bound states depends on well width and depth
  • ✓ Contrast finite-well wavefunction penetration against the infinite well's exact zero at the walls
  • ✓ Identify even vs. odd parity bound states from their wavefunction symmetry
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the "Finite Potential Wells and Barriers" text and the idea of a classically forbidden region
  • ● Ask students to predict whether a shallow, narrow well can always support at least one bound state
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Set V₀ to minimum and confirm exactly one bound state exists, with a visibly leaking wavefunction
  2. Raise V₀ until 3-4 states appear, and record each state's parity and node count
  3. Toggle the infinite-well overlay for the ground state and discuss why the finite-well energy is always somewhat lower
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Connect wavefunction penetration to real confined-carrier devices (quantum wells, doped-atom electrons)
  • ● Preview how generalizing a well to a *barrier* (allowed regions on both sides instead of a well) leads directly into quantum tunneling, covered next
References
  • ● Finite Potential Well — Wikipedia
  • ● Particle in a Box (Infinite Well) — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 2: Quantum Mechanics Foundations — this textbook

docs.title: Forward and Reverse Bias Band Diagram Explorer
docs.text:
Forward and Reverse Bias Band Diagram Explorer

← Back to Chapter 15: The P-N Junction Under Bias

Description

This MicroSim shows how an applied bias \(V\) modifies the equilibrium band diagram of a silicon p-n junction. A live band diagram bends according to the net barrier height \(V_{bi}-V\), a horizontal width bar gives a direct visual read on the depletion width \(W(V)\), and a results card reports the barrier height, depletion width, and doping concentrations as the bias slider moves between reverse and forward bias. Three preset buttons — Reverse Bias, Equilibrium, and Forward Bias — snap the slider to representative values while it stays fully draggable in between.

Key Features

  • ● Live band diagram that bends according to applied bias, color-coded by regime (green = forward, red-orange = reverse, purple = equilibrium)
  • ● Reverse Bias / Equilibrium / Forward Bias presets for one-click jumps to representative bias values, plus a continuously draggable bias slider
  • ● Depletion-width bar that visibly narrows under forward bias and widens under reverse bias, with a reference tick at the equilibrium width
  • ● Content-driven results card reporting \(V_{bi}\), applied bias, barrier height, \(W\), \(N_A\), and \(N_D\)
  • ● Responsive canvas that resizes with the browser window, with a stacked layout on narrow screens
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand / Apply (L2-L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Explain, Calculate

  • ✓ Explain how forward and reverse bias modify the equilibrium band diagram and potential barrier
  • ✓ Calculate depletion width under forward or reverse bias from doping and applied voltage
References
  • ● P-N Junction Biasing — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 15: The P-N Junction Under Bias — this textbook

docs.title: Gauss's Law Explorer
docs.text:
Gauss's Law Explorer

← Back to Chapter 1: Physics and Math Foundations

Description

This MicroSim draws a spherical Gaussian surface (shown as a circle, its 2D cross-section) around a point charge. Changing the surface's radius changes the electric field at the surface, but the total flux \(\Phi_E = Q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0\) stays exactly the same, since it depends only on the enclosed charge. A toggle button moves the charge outside the surface, showing that flux drops to exactly zero when no charge is enclosed.

Key Features

  • ● Radius slider (1 to 5 nm) that visibly changes the field strength but not the total flux
  • ● Charge slider (−5 to +5 nC) showing flux scales directly with enclosed charge
  • ● Inside/outside toggle demonstrating that flux is exactly zero when the charge is not enclosed
  • ● Live numeric readout of enclosed charge, field at the surface, and total flux
How to Use
  1. Drag the radius slider and watch the flux readout stay fixed while the field readout changes
  2. Drag the charge slider and watch flux scale directly with the enclosed charge
  3. Click "Move Charge Outside Surface" and note the flux immediately drops to zero, regardless of radius
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply (L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Calculate, verify

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Apply Gauss's Law to compute total flux from enclosed charge alone
  • ✓ Verify that flux is independent of the Gaussian surface's size or shape
  • ✓ Explain why charge outside a Gaussian surface contributes zero net flux
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review Gauss's Law from the chapter and ask why it is easier to apply than Coulomb's Law for symmetric charge distributions
  • ● Ask students to predict what happens to flux if the radius is doubled
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Double the radius and confirm the flux readout is unchanged while the field readout drops
  2. Double the charge and confirm the flux readout doubles
  3. Move the charge outside and confirm flux reads exactly zero at every radius
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Connect back to Worked Example 10 and Concept Check in the Basic Electromagnetics section
  • ● Preview that Chapter 14 uses this exact technique to find the field inside a p-n junction's depletion region
References
  • ● Gauss's Law — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 1: Gauss's Law — this textbook

docs.title: Gradient, Divergence, and Curl Explorer
docs.text:
Gradient, Divergence, and Curl Explorer

← Back to Chapter 1: Physics and Math Foundations

Description

This MicroSim lets students switch between the three vector-calculus operators introduced in the chapter — gradient, divergence, and curl — and see each one applied to simple preset fields. In Gradient mode, a colored scalar field (a bowl or a saddle) is overlaid with arrows showing \(\nabla V\), the direction of steepest increase. In Divergence and Curl mode, arrows show a vector field, tinted red/blue (source/sink) or purple (rotational) according to the field's constant analytic divergence or curl.

Key Features

  • ● Operator selector switching between Gradient, Divergence, and Curl
  • ● 2-3 preset fields per operator (bowl/saddle for gradient; source/sink/uniform for divergence; rotational/radial/uniform for curl)
  • ● Quiver-plot arrows at grid points showing field/gradient direction and relative magnitude
  • ● Numeric readout of the exact analytic divergence or curl value for the selected field
How to Use
  1. Choose an operator (Gradient, Divergence, or Curl) from the first dropdown
  2. Choose a preset field from the second dropdown, which updates to show only fields relevant to the selected operator
  3. Compare the arrows and background tint between fields, and read the numeric operator value at the bottom of the canvas
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand (L2)  |  Bloom Verb: Interpret, distinguish

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Distinguish which operator takes a scalar field as input and which take a vector field
  • ✓ Recognize a source field (positive divergence) versus a sink field (negative divergence) versus a divergence-free field
  • ✓ Recognize a rotational field (nonzero curl) versus a curl-free radial or uniform field
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the gradient, divergence, and curl definitions and equations from the chapter
  • ● Ask students which operator they expect to give zero for a uniform field
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. In Gradient mode, compare the bowl and saddle fields and note where the arrows point
  2. In Divergence mode, compare the source and sink fields and note the tint color and sign
  3. In Curl mode, compare the rotational and radial fields and note that only one produces a nonzero curl
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Connect the "Source (outward)" field to Gauss's Law: positive divergence corresponds to positive charge density
  • ● Note that the radial field's zero curl matches the chapter's statement that static electric fields are curl-free
References
  • ● Gradient — Wikipedia
  • ● Divergence — Wikipedia
  • ● Curl — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 1: Vector Calculus — this textbook

docs.title: Learning Graph Viewer
docs.text:
Open Learning Graph Viewer

Template for iframe

<iframe src="./main.html" width="100%" height="650px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

This interactive viewer lets you explore all 256 concepts in the Semiconductor Physics learning graph. It is the visual map of the entire course: every concept links back to the chapter and glossary entry that teaches it, the concepts it depends on, the concepts that depend on it, and any related MicroSims.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Search: Type in the search box to find and highlight specific concepts, then click a result to focus on it
  • Category Filtering: Use checkboxes to show/hide the 14 concept categories, or Check All / Uncheck All
  • Node Detail Panel: Click any concept to see its definition, chapter, prerequisites, dependents, Bloom level (where available), related MicroSims, and links to the glossary, quiz, and practice problems
  • Prerequisite/Dependent Highlighting: Selecting a concept highlights its prerequisites (blue edges) and the concepts that depend on it (orange edges), and dims everything else
  • Reset View / Fit to Screen: Toolbar buttons to clear the current selection or re-center the graph
  • Statistics: Live counts of visible nodes, visible edges, total concepts, and foundational concepts
  • Collapsible Sidebar: Automatically collapses on small screens; toggle with the ☰ button

docs.title: Using the Viewer
docs.text:
1. Search for Concepts: Start typing in the search box to find and highlight concepts. Click a result to focus on that node.
  2. Filter by Category: Use the category checkboxes in the sidebar to show or hide groups of related concepts.
  3. Explore a Concept: Click on a node to open its detail panel, then click any prerequisite or dependent chip to jump directly to that concept.
  4. Navigate the Graph: Drag to pan, scroll to zoom, use Fit to Screen to re-center, or Reset View to clear the current selection.
  5. Jump into the Textbook: From the detail panel, follow the links to the concept's chapter, glossary entry, chapter quiz, or practice problems.

docs.title: Graph Structure
docs.text:
• Foundational Concepts (left side): Prerequisites with no dependencies of their own
  • Advanced Concepts (right side): Topics that build on multiple prerequisites
  • Edges: Arrows point from a concept to the prerequisites it depends on

docs.title: Hall Effect Explorer
docs.text:
Hall Effect Explorer

← Back to Chapter 12: Diffusion and Advanced Transport Phenomena

Description

This MicroSim draws a current-carrying semiconductor bar in a perpendicular magnetic field, showing carriers deflected toward one edge by the Lorentz force and the resulting charge accumulation. The computed Hall voltage, \(V_H=R_HIB/t\), and its sign — which flips between hole and electron conduction — are displayed live as the carrier type, current, field, concentration, and thickness sliders change.

Key Features

  • ● Schematic carrier deflection diagram with charge accumulation on both edges
  • ● Live Hall voltage calculation with sign interpretation
  • ● Reversible magnetic field direction and carrier type toggle
  • ● Four sensor design presets
  • ● Responsive canvas that resizes with the browser window
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand / Analyze (L2-L4)  |  Bloom Verb: Explain, Interpret

  • ✓ Explain how the Lorentz force produces a Hall voltage
  • ✓ Interpret Hall voltage sign to identify majority carrier type
References
  • ● Hall Effect — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 12: Diffusion and Advanced Transport Phenomena — this textbook

docs.title: Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle Explorer
docs.text:
Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle Explorer

← Back to Chapter 2: Quantum Mechanics Foundations

Description

This MicroSim lets students adjust the position uncertainty \(\Delta x\) of an electron or proton and see the resulting minimum momentum uncertainty \(\Delta p_{min} = \hbar/(2\Delta x)\) and velocity uncertainty \(\Delta v_{min} = \Delta p_{min}/m\), computed from \(\hbar = 1.0546\times10^{-34}\) J·s. Two Gaussian curves — a position wave packet and a momentum spread — visually narrow and widen in opposite directions as the slider moves, making the trade-off in \(\Delta x\,\Delta p \geq \hbar/2\) immediately visible.

Key Features

  • ● Log-scale Δx slider spanning 1 pm to 1 µm
  • ● Particle-type dropdown (electron or proton) converting \(\Delta p\) into \(\Delta v\)
  • ● Two linked Gaussian curves showing the position wave packet and momentum spread narrowing/widening inversely
  • ● Live numeric readouts of \(\Delta x\), \(\Delta p\), and \(\Delta v\)
How to Use
  1. Drag the \(\Delta x\) slider and watch the position curve narrow while the momentum curve widens
  2. Switch the particle dropdown between electron and proton to compare \(\Delta v_{min}\)
  3. Read the numeric panel to see the exact computed uncertainties
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand / Apply (L2-L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Interpret, Calculate

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Apply \(\Delta x\,\Delta p \geq \hbar/2\) to compute a minimum momentum uncertainty
  • ✓ Interpret the inverse relationship between position and momentum uncertainty visually
  • ✓ Explain why lighter particles (electrons) show larger velocity uncertainty than heavier ones (protons) for the same confinement
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the boxed Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle from the chapter
  • ● Ask students to predict what happens to \(\Delta p\) if \(\Delta x\) is cut in half
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Set \(\Delta x\) to 0.1 nm (roughly atomic scale) and record \(\Delta p\) and \(\Delta v\) for the electron
  2. Switch to the proton at the same \(\Delta x\) and compare \(\Delta v\)
  3. Drag \(\Delta x\) to its smallest value and observe both curves at their most extreme widths
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Discuss why this is a fundamental property of nature, not a limitation of measurement instruments
  • ● Connect this to why confined electrons in a particle-in-a-box have nonzero minimum kinetic energy
References
  • ● Uncertainty Principle — Wikipedia
  • ● Wave Packet — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 2: Quantum Mechanics Foundations — this textbook

docs.title: Hydrogenic Donor/Acceptor Ionization Energy Calculator
docs.text:
Hydrogenic Donor/Acceptor Ionization Energy Calculator

← Back to Chapter 7: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Semiconductors

Description

This MicroSim models a donor's loosely-bound fifth electron as a hydrogen-like system, computing its ionization energy as \(E_D = 13.6\ \text{eV}\times(m^*/m_0)/\varepsilon_r^2\) from adjustable effective-mass-ratio and relative-dielectric-constant sliders. A schematic orbit diagram grows or shrinks alongside the computed energy, and the result is compared directly to real measured donor/acceptor ionization energies in silicon and germanium.

Key Features

  • ● Live hydrogenic ionization energy calculation in meV and eV
  • ● Schematic Bohr-like orbit that scales with the same parameters
  • ● Real measured comparison values for P and B in Si, and P in Ge
  • ● Responsive canvas that resizes with the browser window
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply (L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Calculate, Apply

  • ✓ Apply the hydrogenic-model formula to compute a donor's ionization energy
  • ✓ Explain why effective mass and dielectric screening shrink ionization energy relative to bare hydrogen
References

  • ● Donor (Semiconductors) — Wikipedia

docs.title: Ideal Diode I-V Curve Explorer
docs.text:
Ideal Diode I-V Curve Explorer

← Back to Chapter 15: The P-N Junction Under Bias

Description

This MicroSim plots the ideal diode equation, \(J=J_0(e^{V/V_T}-1)\), in a chosen linear or semi-log view. A saturation current slider, a temperature slider (which sets \(V_T=kT/q\)), and a draggable voltage marker let students explore both the sharp forward "knee" of the linear view and the straight-line forward region of the semi-log view. The chart's three physically-distinct operating regions — Reverse Saturation, Near-Zero Bias, and Exponential Forward Conduction — are shaded directly on the curve and bracketed below the voltage axis, and a "Compare 300K vs T2" mode overlays a second curve at an independently-adjustable second temperature so students can see how temperature reshapes the forward "knee."

Key Features

  • ● Linear and semi-log views of the same underlying I-V curve, with numeric tick marks and labels on both axes
  • ● Labeled operating regions — Reverse Saturation, Near-Zero Bias, and Exponential Forward Conduction — shaded on the chart and bracketed under the x-axis
  • ● Temperature-comparison mode that overlays a second curve at an independently-adjustable second temperature T2 alongside the primary curve fixed at 300 K
  • ● Draggable voltage marker with live current readout and a color-coded operating-region badge
  • ● Responsive canvas that resizes with the browser window
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply (L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Calculate, Interpret

  • ✓ Apply the ideal diode equation to compute current density at a given voltage
  • ✓ Interpret the exponential forward rise and reverse saturation regions of the I-V curve
References
  • ● Shockley Diode Equation — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 15: The P-N Junction Under Bias — this textbook

docs.title: Injection Level Classifier
docs.text:
Injection Level Classifier

← Back to Chapter 13: Non-Equilibrium Carriers and Recombination

Description

This MicroSim compares excess carrier concentration \(\Delta n\) to the equilibrium majority carrier concentration \(n_0\) (set by doping) on a continuous log-scale meter, classifying the ratio \(\Delta n/n_0\) as low-level injection (\(\Delta n\ll n_0\)), a transition band, or high-level injection (\(\Delta n\) comparable to or exceeding \(n_0\)). A needle marks the current ratio, and an explanation box describes which simplifying assumptions are safe to use in each zone.

Key Features

  • ● Continuous injection-level meter (log Δn/n₀) instead of a binary classification
  • ● Explicit transition band where neither the low- nor high-level shortcut is accurate
  • ● Live n₀, Δn, and ratio readout with zone-specific explanation text
  • ● Responsive canvas that resizes with the browser window
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand / Apply (L2-L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Classify, Compare

  • ✓ Classify a given injection scenario as low-level or high-level
  • ✓ Explain which carrier population is perturbed in each regime
References
  • ● Carrier Generation and Recombination — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 13: Non-Equilibrium Carriers and Recombination — this textbook

docs.title: Intrinsic vs. Extrinsic Semiconductor Comparison
docs.text:
Intrinsic vs. Extrinsic Semiconductor Comparison

← Back to Chapter 7: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Semiconductors

Description

This MicroSim places a pure silicon lattice side by side with a lattice containing one substitutional donor atom, and pairs each with a realistic, log-scale carrier-concentration bar chart. The intrinsic lattice shows only rare thermally-broken bonds, while the extrinsic lattice shows a free electron contributed immediately by the donor atom — visually explaining why doped (extrinsic) silicon has roughly a million times more carriers than pure (intrinsic) silicon at room temperature.

Key Features

  • ● Side-by-side lattice and chart updating together on a single dropdown toggle
  • ● Realistic order-of-magnitude carrier concentrations for silicon
  • ● Responsive canvas that resizes with the browser window
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand / Analyze (L2-L4)  |  Bloom Verb: Compare, Explain

  • ✓ Explain why a donor atom contributes a carrier without thermal bond-breaking
  • ✓ Compare the order of magnitude of intrinsic versus extrinsic carrier concentration
References
  • ● Extrinsic Semiconductor — Wikipedia
  • ● Intrinsic Semiconductor — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 7: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Semiconductors — this textbook

docs.title: Intrinsic Semiconductor Explorer
docs.text:
Intrinsic Semiconductor Explorer

← Back to Chapter 7: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Semiconductors

Description

This MicroSim shows a schematic 2D silicon lattice in which every covalent bond has a small, temperature-dependent probability of thermally breaking into a free electron and a hole, and a constant probability of reforming (recombination). Starting the animation and increasing the temperature slider makes the equilibrium number of broken bonds grow sharply, directly visualizing why an intrinsic semiconductor's carrier population is created entirely by thermal energy rather than by doping.

Key Features

  • ● Animated bond breaking and recombination, defaulting to stopped so the intact lattice can be inspected first
  • ● Live broken-bond counter showing the current electron-hole pair population
  • ● Drifting electron markers paired with stationary hole markers at each broken bond
  • ● Temperature slider (100 K – 900 K) controlling the exponential break-rate trend
  • ● Responsive canvas with Start/Stop and Reset controls
How to Use
  1. Inspect the lattice at rest — every bond is intact, and the broken-bond count reads zero
  2. Click Start at the default 300 K and watch bonds occasionally break and reform
  3. Drag the temperature slider toward 900 K and watch the broken-bond count rise sharply
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand (L2)  |  Bloom Verb: Explain, Illustrate

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Explain why breaking a covalent bond always produces one electron and one hole together
  • ✓ Describe qualitatively why intrinsic carrier population grows sharply, not linearly, with temperature
  • ✓ Connect bond-breaking (generation) and bond-reforming (recombination) to an equilibrium carrier population
References
  • ● Intrinsic Semiconductor — Wikipedia
  • ● Electron Hole — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 7: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Semiconductors — this textbook

docs.title: Junction Capacitance Explorer
docs.text:
Junction Capacitance Explorer

← Back to Chapter 14: The P-N Junction at Equilibrium

Description

This MicroSim computes the junction capacitance \(C_j=\varepsilon A/W\) of a silicon p-n junction from doping concentrations, junction area, and reverse bias. A live chart plots \(C_j\) against reverse bias \(V_R\), and a parallel-plate capacitor schematic shows the depletion region visibly widening as reverse bias increases, directly illustrating why \(C_j\) falls.

Key Features

  • ● Live Cj vs. reverse-bias curve with a marker at the current setting
  • ● Parallel-plate capacitor schematic whose plate separation tracks the actual depletion width
  • ● Responsive canvas with a stacked mobile layout, tested at desktop, tablet, and mobile widths
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply (L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Calculate, Explain

  • ✓ Compute junction capacitance from depletion width and junction area
  • ✓ Explain qualitatively why reverse bias decreases junction capacitance

  • ● Varicap (Varactor Diode) — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 14: The P-N Junction at Equilibrium — this textbook

docs.title: Junction Electric Field and Depletion Width Explorer
docs.text:
Junction Electric Field and Depletion Width Explorer

← Back to Chapter 14: The P-N Junction at Equilibrium

Description

This MicroSim solves Poisson's equation for a silicon step junction under the depletion approximation, showing three aligned, stacked charts: the depletion charge density \(\rho(x)\), the resulting triangular junction electric field \(E(x)\), and the electrostatic potential \(\psi(x)\) obtained by integrating the field. Dashed reference lines mark the metallurgical junction \(x=0\), the depletion edges \(-x_p\) and \(x_n\), the total width \(W\), the peak field \(E_{max}\), and the built-in potential \(V_{bi}\) directly on the charts. A draggable marker — spanning the full plotted range, not just the depletion region — reads exact values at any position, and the doping sliders update every quantity live.

Key Features

  • ● Three aligned charts — charge density, electric field, and potential, computed in closed form
  • ● Symmetric / p+–n / p–n+ presets for instantly comparing doping-asymmetry effects
  • ● \(x_p\), \(x_n\), \(W\), \(E_{max}\), and \(V_{bi}\) marked directly on the charts, not just listed numerically
  • ● Full-range position marker synchronized across all three plots, including outside the depletion region
  • ● Responsive canvas with a stacked mobile layout, tested at desktop, tablet, and mobile widths
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply / Analyze (L3-L4)  |  Bloom Verb: Apply, Compare, Interpret

  • ✓ Apply Poisson's equation to the depletion approximation to compute depletion charge density and junction electric field
  • ✓ Calculate depletion widths \(x_n\), \(x_p\), and \(W\) from doping concentrations, and interpret how they split between the two sides
References
  • ● Depletion Region — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 14: The P-N Junction at Equilibrium — this textbook

docs.title: Complete Junction I-V Characteristic Explorer
docs.text:
Complete Junction I-V Characteristic Explorer

← Back to Chapter 15: The P-N Junction Under Bias

Description

This MicroSim is the chapter's single synthesis view of the complete junction I-V characteristic: \(I(V)\approx I_0(e^{V/V_T}-1)\) for \(V>-V_{BR}\), and a rapid, illustrative breakdown current increase for \(V\le-V_{BR}\). A single lightly-doped-side concentration slider \(N\) drives both the estimated breakdown voltage \(V_{BR}\approx\varepsilon E_{crit}^2/(2qN)\) and the saturation current \(J_0\); a voltage-marker slider — whose range is recomputed live from \(V_{BR}\) — sweeps a dot across a log\(|J|\) chart spanning all three regions (reverse breakdown, reverse saturation current, and forward conduction), while a small junction cross-section diagram updates its depletion width, barrier height, current-direction arrow, and dominant mechanism label to match.

A Note on Simplifications

The saturation current \(J_0\) is held near the same order of magnitude used elsewhere in this chapter's MicroSims and only scales mildly (and illustratively) with \(N\). The breakdown-region curve is a smooth, continuous, monotonically-increasing extension of the ideal diode equation chosen to match the chapter's own "rapid breakdown current increase" language — it is not a rigorous avalanche-multiplication (Miller) model. The mini-diagram's depletion width uses a fixed representative \(V_{bi}=0.7\ \text{V}\). These simplifications keep the whole picture numerically consistent with the sibling Ideal Diode I-V Curve Explorer and Reverse Breakdown Mechanism Explorer while staying legible across many orders of magnitude of doping and voltage.

Key Features

  • ● One log|J|-vs-V chart showing forward exponential conduction, reverse saturation, and reverse breakdown together, with labeled regions and numeric axis ticks
  • ● Single doping slider that drives both the breakdown voltage estimate and the saturation current together
  • ● Live voltage-marker slider with a dynamically recomputed range spanning deep breakdown through forward bias
  • ● Junction cross-section mini-diagram showing depletion width, barrier height, current direction, and the dominant mechanism at the current voltage
  • ● Colored region badge (forward = green, reverse = red-orange, breakdown = purple) plus full numeric readouts
  • ● Responsive canvas that stacks the chart, diagram, and readout card vertically on narrow screens
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Analyze / Evaluate (L4-L5)  |  Bloom Verb: Synthesize, Compare, Predict

  • ✓ Synthesize forward conduction, reverse saturation, and reverse breakdown into a single unified I-V picture
  • ✓ Predict which of the three regions a given voltage falls into, and identify the dominant physical mechanism there
  • ✓ Evaluate how doping concentration jointly shifts the breakdown voltage and the depletion width shown in the junction diagram
References
  • ● P-n junction — Wikipedia
  • ● Diode — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 15: The P-N Junction Under Bias — this textbook

docs.title: Kronig-Penney Band Formation Explorer
docs.text:
Kronig-Penney Band Formation Explorer

← Back to Chapter 5: Quantum Mechanics of Periodic Crystals

Description

This MicroSim has four linked views walking from physical setup to final result. Periodic Potential shows the Kronig-Penney square-barrier array V(x) schematically, with the lattice constant a, barrier width b, and barrier height V₀ labeled. Transcendental Equation plots \(P\sin(\alpha a)/(\alpha a)+\cos(\alpha a)\) against \(x=\alpha a\) (proportional to \(\sqrt{E}\)), shading in red every region where the curve exceeds \(\pm1\) and explicitly labeling one allowed band and one forbidden gap. Allowed/Forbidden Bands re-draws the same result as a single labeled energy-axis "band ladder," with each band and gap's width shown numerically. E-k Diagram inverts the same equation (via \(\arccos\), no iterative root-finding required) to plot the resulting allowed energy bands against \(k\), with Brillouin zone boundaries labeled at \(k=\pm n\pi/a\) — click or drag anywhere on a band to read off its exact energy and k value.

Key Features

  • ● Four linked views: periodic potential, transcendental equation, allowed/forbidden band ladder, and E-k diagram
  • ● Explicit ALLOWED/FORBIDDEN labels so meaning never has to be inferred from shading alone
  • ● Draggable E-k readout: click or drag on any band to read its energy and Bloch wavevector k
  • ● Adjustable barrier strength P spanning the free-electron limit (P=0) to strongly gapped bands, updating all four views together
  • ● Brillouin zone boundaries labeled at k = ±π/a, ±2π/a, ... directly on the E-k diagram
  • ● Responsive canvas that resizes with the browser window
How to Use
  1. Start with "Periodic Potential" to see the physical barrier array the model solves
  2. Drag P to 0 in "Transcendental Equation" view and confirm all shading disappears
  3. Switch to "Allowed/Forbidden Bands" and read the numeric width of each band and gap
  4. Switch to "E-k Diagram" and click on a band to read off its (E, k), confirming gaps line up with the labeled zone boundaries
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand / Analyze (L2-L4)  |  Bloom Verb: Interpret, Predict, Analyze

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Interpret the Kronig-Penney transcendental equation and identify forbidden energy regions directly from its plot
  • ✓ Predict how increasing barrier strength affects band gap width
  • ✓ Analyze an E-k band diagram to locate band gaps relative to Brillouin zone boundaries
References

Majority and Minority Carrier Explorer

← Back to Chapter 8: Doping, Ionization, and Temperature Regimes

Description

This MicroSim uses a single slider, \(s=\log_{10}(n/n_i)\), to parametrize doping continuously: electron concentration is \(n=n_i\cdot10^{s}\) and hole concentration is always \(p=n_i^2/n\), so \(np=n_i^2\) holds exactly at every position. A log-scale bar chart shows both concentrations directly, and a schematic (not-to-scale) population panel shows a mix of electron and hole icons whose proportions shift as doping changes. A badge names the majority carrier, and a predict-then-reveal challenge question asks what happens to hole concentration when electron concentration increases 100×.

Key Features

  • ● Single continuous slider spanning strongly p-type through intrinsic to strongly n-type
  • ● Exact np = ni² relationship at every slider position

  • ● Responsive canvas that resizes with the browser window, with fullscreen support

  3. Check the title readout at several positions and confirm n × p never changes

docs.title: Maxwell-Boltzmann Speed Distribution
docs.text:
Maxwell-Boltzmann Speed Distribution

← Back to Chapter 1: Physics and Math Foundations

Description

This MicroSim plots the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution for a representative gas particle (mass close to an N\(_2\) molecule) as a function of temperature. Dragging the temperature slider shows the curve broaden and its peak shift to higher speed, while numeric readouts show the most probable speed, the RMS speed, and the average kinetic energy \(\langle KE\rangle = \tfrac{3}{2}k_BT\) in both joules and electron-volts.

Key Features

  • ● Live-updating curve recomputed on every slider change, from 100 K to 1000 K
  • ● Most-probable-speed and RMS-speed markers shown as labeled dashed vertical lines
  • ● Two one-click presets: Room Temperature (300 K) and Liquid Nitrogen (77 K)
  • ● Numeric readout of average kinetic energy in both joules and electron-volts
How to Use
  1. Drag the temperature slider from 100 K to 1000 K and watch the curve broaden and shift right
  2. Click the two preset buttons to directly compare a cryogenic and a room-temperature condition
  3. Read the numeric panel to see how much the average kinetic energy changes between presets
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand (L2)  |  Bloom Verb: Interpret

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Interpret how raising temperature reshapes the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution
  • ✓ Connect the visual broadening of the curve to the increase in \(\langle KE\rangle = \tfrac{3}{2}k_BT\)
  • ✓ Explain why cooling a device changes the thermal energy available to its carriers
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the kinetic theory of gases and the Boltzmann constant from the chapter
  • ● Ask students to predict how the curve will change if temperature doubles
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Click Liquid Nitrogen (77 K) and note the narrow, left-shifted curve
  2. Click Room Temperature (300 K) and compare the broader, right-shifted curve
  3. Slide up to 1000 K and observe how far the most-probable-speed line moves
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Connect back to Worked Example 12 in the chapter
  • ● Preview that this same statistical reasoning reappears for electrons in Chapters 9–10

docs.title: Metallurgical Junction and Depletion Formation Explorer

Metallurgical Junction and Depletion Formation Explorer

← Back to Chapter 14: The P-N Junction at Equilibrium

Description

This MicroSim is an eight-step guided tour of how a p-n junction forms: separate, individually-neutral p-type and n-type regions are joined at the metallurgical junction, majority carriers diffuse across it and recombine near the interface, leaving fixed ionized dopants uncovered, which forms the equilibrium depletion region with clearly marked boundaries \(-x_p\) and \(x_n\) and a built-in electric field that exactly balances further diffusion. Square symbols (fixed ionized donors/acceptors) and round symbols (mobile electrons/holes) stay visually distinct throughout, and the ion positions never change between steps — only the carrier layer thins out near the junction.

Key Features

  • ● Eight-step guided sequence from separate materials to equilibrium, navigated with Prev/Next buttons and step dots
  • ● Distinct mobile-carrier (round) and fixed-ion (square) symbols showing exactly what moves and what stays behind
  • ● Labeled depletion-region boundaries \(-x_p\), \(x_n\) and a built-in field arrow in the final steps
  • ● Responsive canvas reviewed at desktop, tablet, and mobile widths
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand (L2)  |  Bloom Verb: Explain, Describe

  • ✓ Explain how joining p-type and n-type material initiates carrier diffusion across the metallurgical junction

docs.title: Miller Indices Explorer
docs.text:
Miller Indices Explorer

← Back to Chapter 3: Crystal Lattices and Structures

Description

This MicroSim lets students set integer Miller indices \((h\,k\,l)\) with three sliders and immediately see the corresponding crystal plane shaded and outlined inside a rotatable wireframe unit cell. The plane is computed from the intercept-form equation \(hX+kY+lZ=1\) (in fractional coordinates of the lattice constant \(a\)) and clipped against the cube boundary, so an index of 0 correctly produces a plane parallel to that axis, and negative indices correctly show whether the plane crosses the displayed unit cell at all.

Key Features

  • ● Three integer sliders for h, k, and l, ranging from −3 to 3
  • ● Preset buttons for the common planes (100), (110), (111), and (200)
  • ● Free 3D rotation via p5.js \(\texttt{orbitControl()}\) — click-drag to spin, scroll to zoom
  • ● Live readout panel showing intercepts and a clear message when the plane misses the displayed cell
How to Use
  1. Drag the h, k, l sliders or click a preset button to choose Miller indices
  2. Click and drag anywhere on the 3D view to rotate the cell and inspect the plane's orientation
  3. Scroll or pinch to zoom in and out
  4. Read the panel below the canvas for the current intercepts and Miller notation
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply (L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Compute, Construct

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Compute a plane's axis intercepts from its Miller indices and vice versa
  • ✓ Construct and visually verify the (100), (110), (111), and (200) planes inside a unit cell
  • ✓ Explain why an index of 0 means the plane runs parallel to that axis
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the definition of a crystal plane and the intercept-reciprocal procedure for finding Miller indices
  • ● Ask students to sketch what they expect the (110) plane to look like before opening the MicroSim
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Click through all four presets in order and describe how the shaded polygon's shape changes
  2. Set one index to 0 and confirm the plane becomes parallel to that axis, extending to the cell boundary
  3. Try a negative index and observe the readout panel's message when the plane no longer crosses the displayed cell
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Have students compute the Miller indices for a plane with given intercepts by hand and verify with the sliders
  • ● Discuss how Miller planes like (111) relate to the tetrahedral bonding directions seen in the diamond cubic MicroSim
References
  • ● Miller Index — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 3: Crystal Lattices and Structures — this textbook

Particle in a Box Explorer

← Back to Chapter 2: Quantum Mechanics Foundations

Description

This MicroSim lets students adjust the box width \(L\) (0.1 nm to 5 nm) and quantum number \(n\) (1 to 6) of an electron confined to an infinite square well, plotting the wavefunction \(\psi_n(x) = \sqrt{2/L}\sin(n\pi x/L)\) and the probability density \(|\psi_n(x)|^2\). A side-panel energy-level ladder computed from \(E_n = n^2h^2/(8m_eL^2)\) shows that energy levels are not evenly spaced — they scale as \(n^2\).

Key Features

  • ● Box width slider from 0.1 nm to 5 nm
  • ● Integer quantum-number slider for n = 1 through 6, extended down through n = 0 and to n = -6 for exploration
  • ● Overlaid ψₙ(x) and |ψₙ(x)|² plots with internal nodes marked
  • ● Energy-level ladder diagram for E₁ through E₆, with the selected level highlighted
How to Use
  1. Drag the n slider and count how the number of internal nodes changes
  2. Drag the L slider and watch every level in the energy ladder shift
  3. Compare the highlighted level to the other five to see the n² spacing pattern
  4. Drag n below 1 to see why n = 0 and negative n are excluded from (or redundant with) the physical spectrum
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply / Analyze (L3-L4)  |  Bloom Verb: Calculate, Distinguish

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Apply \(\psi_n(x)=\sqrt{2/L}\sin(n\pi x/L)\) to sketch stationary states of a confined particle
  • ✓ Analyze how \(E_n \propto n^2/L^2\) produces unevenly spaced energy levels
  • ✓ Distinguish the wavefunction from the probability density it produces
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the boxed particle-in-a-box wavefunction and energy formulas from the chapter
  • ● Ask students to predict how many nodes ψ₄ will have before checking
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Step n from 1 to 6 at fixed L and record each internal node count
  2. Fix n = 2 and shrink L from 5 nm to 0.1 nm, noting how quickly E₂ rises
  3. Compare the E₁-E₂ gap to the E₅-E₆ gap in the ladder diagram
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Drag n to 0 live and discuss why it is not a valid state (it would mean no particle at all); drag to a negative n and discuss why it duplicates its positive counterpart rather than describing a new state
  • ● Preview how this quantized-level structure foreshadows the energy bands built from many confined electrons later in the course

Quantum Tunneling Probability Explorer

← Back to Chapter 2: Quantum Mechanics Foundations

Description

This MicroSim lets students adjust a rectangular barrier's height ratio \(V_0/E\) (1.1 to 5) and width \(L\) (0.1 nm to 2 nm) for an electron with fixed energy \(E=1\) eV, and see the simplified tunneling approximation \(T \approx e^{-2\kappa L}\), \(\kappa = \sqrt{2m_e(V_0-E)}/\hbar\) update live. A schematic wavefunction shows an oscillating incident/reflected wave, an exponentially decaying curve inside the barrier, and a reduced-amplitude transmitted wave beyond it.

Key Features

  • ● Barrier height ratio slider (V₀/E from 1.1 to 5) with fixed particle energy E = 1 eV
  • ● Barrier width slider from 0.1 nm to 2 nm
  • ● Schematic wavefunction: oscillating (incident+reflected) — decaying (barrier) — oscillating (transmitted)
  • ● Live transmission-probability readout and gauge bar (√T-scaled so tiny probabilities remain visible)
How to Use
  1. Drag the V₀/E slider and watch the decay curve inside the barrier steepen as the barrier gets relatively taller
  2. Drag the barrier width slider and watch T fall rapidly as the barrier widens
  3. Read the numeric T value and gauge bar to judge the transmission probability
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply / Understand (L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Calculate, Interpret

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Apply \(T \approx e^{-2\kappa L}\) to estimate tunneling probability through a rectangular barrier
  • ✓ Interpret why T falls off exponentially with both barrier width and height
  • ✓ Recognize the limits of the simplified approximation (valid when \(\kappa L \gg 1\))
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)

  • ● Ask students to predict whether doubling barrier width or doubling (V0/E − 1) will hurt transmission more

  2. Increase L to 2 nm at the same V₀/E and compare
  3. Reset L to 0.1 nm and raise V₀/E to 5, comparing the new T to the very first reading
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Discuss real-world tunneling devices (tunnel diodes, scanning tunneling microscopes, flash memory)
  • ● Preview how tunneling reappears later in the course when discussing thin oxide layers in MOS junctions

At zero injection the two levels coincide, drawn as one combined \(E_{Fn}=E_{Fp}=E_F\) line; as injection increases, they animate smoothly apart, with a labeled vertical bracket showing the split \(\Delta E_F=E_{Fn}-E_{Fp}\) directly on the diagram.

  • ● ΔE_F bracket — a labeled double-headed arrow drawn directly between the two levels
  • ● n-type / p-type doping selector and an information card with n, p, Δn, both quasi-Fermi offsets, the split, and the injection regime (low/transition/high-level)

Reciprocal Lattice and Brillouin Zone Explorer

← Back to Chapter 5: Quantum Mechanics of Periodic Crystals

Description

This MicroSim has two linked views. The Real vs. Reciprocal Lattice view renders a real-space 2D lattice side by side with its reciprocal lattice, each with its primitive vectors (\(\vec a_1,\vec a_2\) and \(\vec b_1,\vec b_2\)) drawn from a highlighted origin point, and the first Brillouin zone boundary overlaid directly on the reciprocal panel. Lattice constants \(a_x, a_y\) (in nanometers) are independently adjustable, an optional rotation slider turns both lattices together, and numerical real-space and reciprocal-space spacing values (in both nm-1 and m-1) update live and animate smoothly, making the inverse relationship \(2\pi/a\) directly visible rather than just stated. The Wigner-Seitz Construction view zooms in on the first Brillouin zone construction itself — drawing the perpendicular bisector lines to the nearest reciprocal lattice points and shading the enclosed region — with a small real-space Wigner-Seitz inset for direct comparison to Chapter 3's primitive-cell construction.

Key Features

  • ● Primitive vectors a₁, a₂ and reciprocal vectors b₁, b₂ drawn from a highlighted origin, with nearest-neighbor lattice points highlighted
  • ● First Brillouin zone boundary overlaid directly on the reciprocal lattice panel, not just in a separate view
  • ● Independently adjustable a_x, a_y (nm) plus an optional rotation slider that turns both lattices together
  • ● Live numerical readout of real-space and reciprocal-space spacing in nm⁻¹ and m⁻¹, animated toward each new value
  • ● Wigner-Seitz construction with dashed perpendicular-bisector lines, a shaded first Brillouin zone, and a real-space comparison inset
  • ● Responsive canvas that resizes with the browser window
How to Use
  1. In "Real vs. Reciprocal Lattice" view, drag a_x and watch the numerical readout and reciprocal spacing shrink together as real-space spacing grows
  2. Select "Rectangular lattice" and stretch a_x independently of a_y
  3. Drag the rotation slider and confirm the primitive vectors, reciprocal vectors, and Brillouin zone all rotate together
  4. Switch to "Wigner-Seitz Construction" and compare the real-space inset to the reciprocal-space construction
